#9186. The Greatest Art Costumes From Hyperallergic's Halloween Party

From “Las Dos Fridas” to a walking Eva Hesse sculpture, Hyperallergic members, readers, friends, and artists brought the spirit of the season to our second annual costume contest.

A Dutch still life, “Beast Jesus,” several esoteric Goya characters, and not one but two Marina Abramović/Ulay references (and not even the most obvious ones!) walk into a bar ... That’s a Hyperallergic Halloween, baby!

On Wednesday evening, October 28, almost 200 of our members, readers, artists, supporters, and their enthusiastic friends rolled into Oberon in Brooklyn for our annual art costume party. Winners in several categories ranging from “Best in Show” to “Most Likely to Get Censored in Florida” brought out the art-history nerd within them, materializing into both immediately recognizable icons — Roy Lichtenstein's “Drowning Girls” and Johannes Vermeer’s “Girl with a Pearl Earring” — and admirably obscure references (oh, she was an Eva Hesse rope sculpture?!).

We’re so grateful to our absurdly smart, creative, and crafty community for their commitment to the bit. And a big shout-out to Zac Thompson for their incredible photographs, which will help us relive the night for many moons, or at least as we wait impatiently for next year ... 🌝

Best in Show winners Emilio Rojas and Chico Raro as Pedro Lemebel and Francisco Casa Silva of Las Yeguas del Apocalipsis’s “Las Dos Fridas” (1989). No bribing was necessary to convince the panel.

Zoë Lescaze and Michael Rossi made every part of their costumes from scratch — yes, including the chair — to dress as lesser-known characters from Francisco Goya's Los caprichos (1797–98) series. The couple was among the winners of the "Most Esoteric" award, naturally.

Richard Prince's "Wayward Nurse" (2005), part of the artist's series critiquing the sexualization of nurses on pulp-fiction book covers, would not fly in the Sunshine State in 2026!

Curators and staff from the Heckscher Museum of Art in Huntington, New York, recreated a painting from the institution's own collection: George Grosz's antifascist "Eclipse of the Sun" (1926).

Melissa Brown and Marie Lorenz won over the crowd as none other than the infamously botched “Ecce Homo” aka “Beast Jesus” and its author, restorer Cecilia Giménez Zueco!

Hyperallergic Co-founders Veken Gueyikian and Hrag Vartanian with one of this year's costume contest judges, Nicholas D. Lowry, president of Swann Auction Galleries. Veken is Kazimir Malevich’s “Black Square” (1915), and Vartanian is a 17th-century Dutch still life painting — check out the skull! (Memento mori, very Halloween-coded.)

Our wonderful costume contest judges! Left to right: New York Democratic Congressional candidate Claire Valdez, artist Jia Sung as the Spirit of Spirit Airlines (aka what everyone used to take to get to Art Basel Miami Beach), critic Aruna D’Souza in sleek black feathers, and Nicholas D. Lowry as a fashionable pumpkin in plaid.

Hyperallergic Staff Writer Anna Lee as Johannes Vermeer’s “Girl with a Pearl Earring” (c. 1665) — an art-history classic, made otherworldly by photographer Zac Thompson’s expert double exposure.

These guests brought Museo del Prado right to your doorstep as a rather gory version of Francisco Goya's “Saturn Devouring His Son” (1820–23). Body horror!

Artist Coco Fusco donned one of the fabulous works in Marisol's wearable wooden sculpture "Three Women with Umbrella" (1965–66). Who says Pop art is dead?

If we had a “Cutest” category this year, this pawesome group would have taken the gold! Left to right: Will Swanson, Dwai, Cosette Patterson, Lauren Blaser, Shelby Roller, Sophia Tedesco, and Daniela Alonso as Cassius Marcellus Coolidge’s “A Friend in Need” (1903).

Emily Dotsikas of Alma Communications as Roy Lichtenstein’s “Drawing Girl” (1963). Brad, who?

Hyperallergic Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara addresses the crowd after a very competitive contest. Just don't ask him what his costume is!

Marina Abramović and Ulay’s “Rest Energy” (1980). There’s nothing scarier than a multi-year situationship, except maybe literally putting your heart in the hands of your lover.

Hyperallergic Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar went as Snoopy for the fourth year in a row, a costume she calls her “magnum opus.”

“I made this Snoopy costume with stuff that I already had at home — the ears, spot, and tail were from an old black tee; I painted an old beauty blender black and used it as Snoopy's nose,” Nayyar shared. “My love of this cartoon beagle is well-known and documented. I'm already a crazy dog lady, but there's something about Snoopy's cheeky attitude and ridiculous antics that flips the script on the ‘man's best friend’ marker, which I find really liberating and inspirational.”

Artist agent Anna Staub (left) and curator and gallerist Yuna Cabon of Third Born (right) joined forces, quite literally, to embody Marina Abramović and Ulay’s “Relation in Time” (1977).

What still life is complete without its peckish butterfly? Houry Geudelekian and Hyperallergic Co-founder and Editor-at-Large Hrag Vartanian make a perfect pair.

Us: “What are you?”Artist Danielle De Jesus: “I'm a broke MFA student!”

Just brilliant, down to the Whitney Museum artist lifetime pass!

Hyperallergic contributors Julie Schneider (middle) as a Keith Haring subway drawing and Daniela Mayer (far right) as an AI girlfriend, with Felix Moody as water and Brian Henderson as Candy Warhol (not pictured: candy corn costume).

Artists Jesse Lambert as Ray Johnson and Linda Ganjian as Eva Hesse's rope sculpture "No title" (1970). Is this what they mean by a two-person show?

Writer Jennifer Samet of Hyperallergic's beloved “Beer With a Painter” column arrived as the ultimate tastemaker: Peggy Guggenheim.

Cheryl Hageman, deputy director of MTA Arts & Design, as a painting from Georgia O'Keeffe's Sky Above Clouds (1960–77) series.

#9185. To Live Is to Believe

Remembering Ursula von Rydingsvard, an Epstein survivor’s message for MoMA, interviews with Paul Pfeiffer and Layli Long Soldier, and the best costumes of our artsy Halloween party.

On a fair afternoon in Queens, New York, a woman in a red dress crosses the street in front of me with an actual axe under her arm. Her face is stern, her step fast, and you can tell from the blood on her axe that she wasn’t using it to chop wood. A police siren wails in the distance, but that doesn’t seem to bother her.

I reach to lock the car and then remember it’s Halloween.

At a warm and lovely dinner at Cabinet Magazine, founder and editor-in-chief Sina Najafi shows us a photograph of tightrope walker Margret Zimmermann balancing on a high wire above the bombed-out ruins of the Haymarket in Cologne, Germany, in 1946. She looks her finest in her red lipstick, but a treacherous wind is blowing in her hair as a crowd watches from far below.

Outside, Brooklyn seems to be getting richer and poorer at the same time. A man wearing a bejeweled crown asks me for money. In this city, performance artists are beggars and beggars are performance artists.

At Hyperallergic’s art-themed Halloween party, dozens of guests show up with impressive costumes and really commit to the act. Claire Valdez, an artist and organizer who’s running for Congress, drops by and serves as a judge in our art costume contest. I don’t have a costume, but I perform all night.

“To live is to believe,” Marcel Duchamp says in a video on my phone screen. A little girl dressed as Lady Liberty crosses the street with her mother, a torch in her hand. She keeps the torch held high as they walk off, and that makes me smile.

A Dutch still life, “Beast Jesus,” several esoteric Goya characters, and not one but two Marina Abramović/Ulay references (and not even the most obvious ones!) walk into a bar ... #9184. Minimalist House in Japan by FORM/Kouichi Kimura is "reduced to the essentials"

Photography by Norihito Yamauchi

A monochrome palette and pared-back, open interiors define the aptly named Minimalist House, a home in Japan designed by local studio FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects.

Located in Shiga prefecture, the 73-square-metre home is formed of cubic volumes clad in corrugated metal and black render, perched on a hill overlooking the nearby Lake Biwa.

Minimalist House was designed for a single occupant, but FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects wanted to challenge the assumption that this would mean small-feeling interiors.

This led the studio to create a series of voids and long sightlines that it said help to “liberate space”.

“When hearing ‘a home for a single occupant’, people typically imagine a compact house,” founder Kouichi Kimura told Dezeen.

“Here, living alone is regarded not as a spatial constraint, but as a condition that liberates space,” he added.

“Starting from the individual as the base unit, the house explores a new way of single-person living through the minimal composition reduced to the essentials, with the space that invites in the surrounding view, light, wind, and sound.”

The plan of Minimalist House revolves around a tall void cut through its centre, which extends upwards into a skinny, double-height volume projecting from its roof with a large window.

Finished with grey-plastered walls and dark stone floors, a kitchen, dining space and study occupy the ground floor, with metal and concrete steps leading up to a living space and bedroom above.

Facing the road, the front of the home has been left almost entirely blank. Instead, the interiors open up on the opposite side towards views of the lake in the distance, with the dining table, study and bed pushed up against large, deep-set windows.

“Each floor is designed as a single open layout,” explained Kimura. “The double-height space vertically connects the upper and lower levels. Manipulating floor and ceiling levels gently articulates each space without clearly dividing them.”

“The living space on the upper level is designed not only for daily life, but also for enjoying music. Within the double-height volume, sound resonates off the walls and ceiling, filling the entire space,” he added.

A glass corridor with sliding doors separates the main home from a single-storey washroom, which the studio introduced to ensure that this everyday passage would capture views out over the lake.

“Placing these wet areas away from the main structure creates a natural flow of movement in daily life,” Kimura explained.

“Walking through the glazed corridor in between allows one to touch the landscape, light, and breeze, offering a gentle transition in the everyday time,” he added.

Minimalist forms and interiors often feature in the work of FORM/Kouichi Kimura Architects, with the studio’s previous projects in Shiga including a blocky hair salon and home and a skinny home with carefully-placed windows to avoid overlooking.

Photography by Norihito Yamauchi

#9180. New research reveals original colours of Ancient Egyptian shrine at Oxford museum

A digital projection will recolour the Shrine of Taharqa © Fisher Studios, 2026; courtesy Ashmolean Museum, University of Oxford

A shrine built almost 3,000 years ago in northern Sudan will regain its original glowing colour later this month. Housed at the Ashmolean museum in Oxford, and the only freestanding building in Britain dating back to the time of the pharaohs, the Shrine of King Taharqa (690BC-654BC) will be recoloured through a digital projection that has been made after extensive research on surviving scraps and traces of pigment.

Fragments of red paint survive in crevices of the sandstone carvings, but microscopic analysis and hyperspectral imaging—combining photography and spectroscopy—also revealed evidence of colours now invisible to the naked eye, including yellow and “Egyptian blue”, a brilliant pigment used to depict divine figures.

According to Liam McNamara, the Ashmolean's keeper of antiquities, the carvings and inscriptions tell the story of the construction of the shrine: how the young Taharqa, later the king of Kush in Nubia and Pharaoh of Egypt, saw the ruins of the earlier brick temple to Amun-Re, built by Tutankhamen, with “the sand drifted to its roof”, as he journeyed north towards Thebes. At Taharqa's coronation he vowed to restore it and went on to build the shining new shrine within a new temple. Scorch marks on the stones of the shrine, also revealed in the project, bear witness to its eventual destruction in turn.

The Shrine of King Taharqa Courtesy of Ashmolean Museum, University of Oxford

The relief carved sandstone blocks were originally plastered and brightly painted, showing Taharqa with the gods of Memphis, Heliopolis and also Amun-Re represented as both a Theban and a local Gematen deity. Taharqa himself is depicted both as an Egyptian pharaoh wearing the Double Crown of Upper and Lower Egypt, and in other scenes as a Kushite king with a ram’s head and sun disc earrings and the Kushite crown surmounted by two cobras.

The Shrine of King Taharqa came to Oxford from Khartoum in 150 crates 90 years ago as a gift from the Sudanese government to the Oxford University Excavations in Nubia, which had excavated it and other monuments over several seasons. It was given to the museum in 1936 by Nora Griffith, in memory of her husband Francis Llewellyn Griffith, who had led—and largely paid for—the expeditions. He had taught himself Ancient Egyptian at Oxford since there was no department, and went on to become the first professor of Egyptology and a renowned scholar.

McNamara describes the monument itself as a fascinating insight into the art and archaeology of ancient Sudan.“The new projection—and the scientific research behind it—will allow visitors to appreciate and understand the shrine’s original painted decoration like never before,” he adds

The project has been supported by James Lupton, the Ashmolean's chair of the board of visitors and his wife Béatrice. The projection onto the shrine will be free for all visitors to the Ashmolean’s Ancient Egypt and Sudan galleries, from 13 November.

#9178. Barbara Takenaga’s ‘Awestruck’

At Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art, 40 paintings invite viewers into an exhibition where scale, pattern, and perception are explored and celebrated.

On view at Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art in Kansas City through April 11, 2027, Barbara Takenaga: Awestruck presents the artist’s first comprehensive survey in nearly a decade. Bringing together 40 works spanning her career since the early 2000s, the exhibition reveals the many approaches to abstraction that have shaped Takenaga’s practice. The exhibition is organized by Jessica May, Ph.D., Executive Director, Kemper Museum of Contemporary Art, and Tae Edell, Independent Curator.

The exhibition examines Barbara Takenaga’s intricate compositions through four thematic sections: an emphasis on process, a masterful confusion of scale, an embrace of illusion, and reverent nods to art history. Together, these strategies work to upend the viewer’s expectations, engaging imagination and stoking curiosity for more.

Featuring works from institutional and private collections across the nation, this exhibition includes paintings up to her most recent, revealing Takenaga’s continued push to further her approach across increasingly expanding canvases, opening new paths within her ongoing exploration of abstraction.

The decision between writing your own will and hiring an attorney is not about cost — it is about complexity. A DIY will is perfectly appropriate for a large percentage of Americans, but certain situations demand professional legal counsel.

If your situation falls into the DIY-appropriate category — which covers roughly 70-80% of American households — you can create a legally valid will for free or under $200 in about 30 minutes.

The online legal services market has matured significantly, and several platforms now produce wills that are functionally equivalent to what a basic estate planning attorney would draft. Here is a detailed comparison of the leading options:

Our recommendation for most FI-focused households: Trust & Will offers the best balance of comprehensiveness and value. The $159 individual plan ($259 for couples) includes your will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney — the three essential documents every adult needs. FreeWill is excellent if you want a basic will at zero cost and do not need power of attorney or trust options.

All of these services work the same way: you answer a series of guided questions about your family, assets, beneficiaries, and wishes. The platform generates a state-specific legal document that you print, sign in front of witnesses, and store. The questionnaire approach actually reduces errors compared to attorney-drafted wills because the software forces you to address every required element.

A legally valid will must contain specific elements. Missing any of them can result in your will being thrown out by a probate court, which means your assets are distributed according to your state's default intestacy laws — not your wishes.

Your will does not control assets with named beneficiaries. Life insurance proceeds, 401(k) and IRA accounts, joint bank accounts, and property held in joint tenancy all pass directly to the named beneficiary or surviving co-owner regardless of what your will says. This is the single most important point that DIY will makers must understand. If your 401(k) beneficiary form names your ex-spouse, your ex-spouse gets the money — even if your will says otherwise. Review ALL beneficiary designations as part of your estate planning process.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The number one estate planning mistake for people building wealth is outdated beneficiary designations on retirement accounts and life insurance policies. Your will does NOT override these. If you changed jobs, got married, divorced, or had children since you last updated your 401(k) and IRA beneficiary forms, update them today. This single action prevents more estate planning disasters than any other — and it costs nothing.

Holographic wills are recognized in about 25 states including California, Texas, Virginia, and North Carolina. They must be entirely in your handwriting, signed, and dated. However, they are far more likely to be challenged in probate because they lack witnesses and often contain vague or incomplete instructions. A typed, witnessed will from an online service is always more reliable than a handwritten one, even in states that accept holographic wills.

No. You do not file or register your will while you are alive. The will is submitted to probate court after your death by your executor. During your lifetime, store the original in a secure, accessible location and tell your executor where to find it. Some states allow you to file the will with the court for safekeeping, but this is optional and not required for validity.

Review your will every 3-5 years and update it after any major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a beneficiary or executor, significant change in assets, or moving to a new state. A codicil (amendment) can handle minor changes, but for major revisions, creating an entirely new will is cleaner and reduces the risk of confusion or legal challenge.

Yes. All major online will makers include guardian nomination for minor children. This is one of the most important reasons to have a will — without one, a court will decide who raises your children based on state law, which may not align with your wishes. Name a primary guardian and an alternate, and discuss your decision with the chosen guardians before finalizing the document.

If you die without a will (intestate), your state laws determine who inherits your assets. Typically, everything goes to your spouse and children in proportions set by state statute — which may not match your wishes. Unmarried partners receive nothing. Close friends and favorite charities receive nothing. The court appoints an administrator (who may not be the person you would choose) and the probate process takes longer and costs more. For parents of minor children, the court also decides guardianship.

Writing a will without a lawyer is straightforward, affordable, and legally valid for the majority of American households. Online will makers like Trust & Will ($159) and FreeWill (free) produce state-specific documents in 15-30 minutes that cover everything a basic estate needs. The key to a valid DIY will is proper witnessing, specific beneficiary language, and a residuary clause. Just as importantly, review and update the beneficiary designations on all your retirement accounts and life insurance policies — these override your will and are the most common source of estate planning failures. The only thing worse than a bad will is no will at all. Do it this month.

#9174. Ana Mendieta's Lasting Imprint on Art

A major survey at Tate Modern asks us to take notice of the earth, the power of the female body, and the artist’s remarkable practice.

LONDON — Barely there but deftly constructed, Ana Mendieta’s Siluetas could be anywhere. Some are almost invisible in her documentary photographs. In one from 1979, a human form is impressed into the mud among similar natural shapes on a dried-out riverbank. In another from 1978, a few shimmering leaves, flowers, and branches sketch out the ghost of a woman against a dark tree trunk. Ana Mendieta, a major survey exhibition at Tate Modern, however, asks us to take notice: of the earth, the power of the female body, and the artist’s remarkable practice.

The exhibition eschews a chronological approach, opting to organize works according to their physical and metaphorical places, such as The Grove, The School, or The Sacred Grounds. This effectively points visitors towards the essential site-specificity of Mendieta’s practice; individual works are made in dialogue with particular locations of personal, ecological, or spiritual significance. More broadly, as the wall text explains, Mendieta described her practice as an “attempt to return to the maternal source,” in response to being “cast from the womb (Nature)” through her exile from Cuba as a child.

The exhibition opens with “The Cave,” featuring late works from the 1980s, including her very last video piece “Ochún” (1981) and a selection of her “rupestrian” sculptures inspired by prehistoric rock art. Whereas her more famous Silueta series generally features an imprint or silhouette of Mendieta’s own body, these lesser-known later works are more open-ended in style. Here, female forms are borrowed not from the artist’s anatomy but from the natural forms of rocks and prehistoric representations of goddesses.

#9173. Objects reinstalled at Museo Nacional de Colombia following removal by right-wing government

Several items were removed from this display on 15 October Photo: Angie Matiz

Bogotá’s Museo Nacional de Colombia has reinstalled the 63 objects previously taken down from its permanent galleries over claims of “political indoctrination”. The move followed a court order that reversed the national government's removal of the items on 15 October.

On the evening of 28 October, César Enrique Osorio Ortiz—a judge at Bogotá’s 24th Family Court—ordered Colombia’s cultural ministry and the museum to return the works to their original locations within 48 hours. The ministry complied with the order on Friday (30 October).

The decision came in response to a constitutional-rights case filed by cultural groups and political opponents who had accused the government of the country's far-right President Abelardo de la Espriella of censorship. The judge also ordered both institutions not to remove works based on their content or the views they express.

Among the removed pieces were a pride flag belonging to the activist Elizabeth Castillo, a pen made from a bullet that was used to sign the 2016 peace agreement between the state and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, and a poster for the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women.

Empty spaces where items had been removed from the museum walls Courtesy Colombia Diversa

The removals came amid calls by De la Espriella for a “cultural war” and a “direct blow to ‘wokeism’ and the ideologisation of culture”, an offensive that affected the country’s main museum.

The government’s decision sparked a series of protests during which hundreds of people gathered outside the museum, as well as a joint statement by six museums expressing “deep concern” and calling for the protection of their professional autonomy. The signatories included the Modern art museums of Bogotá, Barranquilla, Cartagena, Medellín and Tolima, as well as the Museo Rayo.

Marielsa Castro Vizcarra, the chief curator of the Museo de Arte Moderno de Medellín (which signed the joint statement), tells The Art Newspaper that the cultural sector responded quickly, from street protests to the statement and the involvement of the International Committee for Museums and Collections of Modern Art. Castro described the incident as “a precedent we need to take into account” and “an authoritarian way of spreading fear”.

According to the judge's ruling, the artefacts had been removed “without a documented curatorial justification” in a decision that “disregarded the constitutional protection of cultural expressions”. The court did not rule out future changes to the exhibitions, provided they are properly justified and not based on the authorities’ objections to the works’ content.

“No government owns our history!” wrote Gabriel Becerra, a left-wing lawmaker behind the constitutional-rights case, in a post on X welcoming the court’s decision.

#9172. How Former Theater Kid James Talarico Stands Up for the Arts in Texas

As Republicans exert an ever-tightening grip on creative freedom in the state, the Democratic Senate hopeful stands out for his track record on arts funding.

Every United States election season, a few candidates capture national attention. This year, one of those names is Democrat James Talarico, who is running for Senate against Republican Ken Paxton. A former theater kid turned language arts teacher now serving his fourth term in the Texas House of Representatives, Talarico would become the first Democrat elected US Senator since the 1980s if he wins.

Talarico has largely built his platform tackling education, a tough battle in a state that has seen eight school district takeovers since 2020. Among the bills he has co-authored is one that focuses on fine arts funding for public schools. Over the past years, the Texas arts scene has sat at the nexus between funding cuts and censorship.

First brought up in 2023 and subsequently reintroduced in 2025, the bill would have been the first of its kind in Texas, had it passed.

“This means hundreds of millions of dollars in new funding for music, dance, art, and theater programs! It’s a game changer,” Talarico, who has an endorsement from the Actors’ Equity Association, wrote on X in 2023. Hyperallergic has contacted Talarico’s campaign for comment.

Before earning his degrees in government and education, Talarico participated in his high school’s theater program, playing two leading roles: Danny Zuko in Grease and Aslan in The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe.

“Research shows fine arts programs improve student achievement, graduation rates, and mental health,” Talarico continued in his post. “I know it did for me when I was growing up.”

Austin-based artist Jean-Pierre Verdijo told Hyperallergic that he’s intrigued by Talarico’s overall message, which he views as focused on fair governance as opposed to fighting another party.

#9171. Herzog & de Meuron and Field Operations release visuals of Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity

Master plan designs for the Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity museum in California have been released, showing galleries connected via a bridge in an adapted 1960s warehouse and a landscape designed by Field Operations.

The updated design for the property in Novato, California, includes the 400-foot-long Great Hall, which the studios said will be “one of the largest single-span spaces for art installations in the country”, a 275-seat theatre, a Japanese-inspired garden and children’s play spaces.

The Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity (the Eames Institute) bought the 88.5-acre property in 2025 to establish a public exhibition space and museum for its collection of furniture and other objects designed by architects Charles and Ray Eames.

The site includes a sawtooth-roofed warehouse and office building designed by architects Jan Lubicz-Nycz and John Savage Bolles, which were originally built for the McGraw-Hill publishing company in 1965.

Shoe company Birkenstock USA operated out of the site until 2019. The Eames Institute now plans to adapt the landscape and buildings for the project.

Architecture studios Herzog & de Meuron and EHDD were signed onto the project when it was first announced last year, and with this most recent update, Field Operations has been announced as the landscape designer.

“What makes this place so extraordinary is the relationship between its remarkable architecture and the landscape of Marin County,” said Field Operations partner Richard Kennedy.

“We imagined the grounds as a living extension of the museum. The idea is simple: ten landscapes, hundreds of places, and infinite journeys.”

According to the team, the warehouse will contain galleries, maker spaces, a theatre and a cafe, while the former office building will be converted into a pavilion for events.

Visitors will enter the warehouse building past a fountain, into a “warm, wood-clad space” containing admissions and the museum shop.

A grand stair will lead to a 120-foot polished stainless-steel bridge that traverses the gallery spaces below. The renders show the spaces as largely open-plan, with the enormous concrete bevels of the roof exposed above.

Other spaces, such as wood and ceramic workshops, will be distributed throughout the building. According to the team, the material palette will primarily consist of colour-stained plywood and plaster, and aluminium windows to “create a dialogue between old and new”.

For the landscape, Field Operations looked to an original plan by landscape architect Tito Patri, which used berms to help bury the buildings into their surroundings, buffering them from a highway which runs directly in front of the site.

The design includes a reconfigured parking and arrival sequence, gardens to the north and south of the warehouse, native stormwater gardens and custom furniture designed by the studio.

Overall, the masterplan will “transform what was once a private, truck-oriented industrial campus into a public cultural destination”, according to the team.

“For my grandparents, design was always grounded in curiosity and intention – looking closely, asking questions, embracing constraints, and finding beauty in the practical and the functional,” said Eames Institute co-founder Llisa Demetrios.

“The museum carries that spirit forward, and it feels especially meaningful to do so in a building that asked us to do the same: work within a remarkable existing structure to imagine what else it can become,” she continued.

Groundbreaking is expected for 2028, with openings projected to begin in 2030.

The project has garnered some criticism for being backed by Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia, who was appointed America’s first Chief Design Officer in 2025 under President Donald Trump.

Dezeen spoke to Gebbia about the appointment in 2025.

The Eames Institute was founded in 2023 and opened a California headquarters in 2024. San Francisco-based design agency Manual created its current brand identity and logo around the same time.

#9170. French Galleries Accuse Art Basel Paris of "Disrespect, Even Contempt"

A group representing over a quarter of the exhibitors released a letter demanding compensation following the fair's abrupt closure.

Five days after Art Basel Paris announced it would prematurely terminate its 2026 edition on October 23, the Comité Professionnel des Galeries d’Art (CPGA), an industry group representing over a quarter of the fair's exhibitors, issued a letter demanding fair compensation and accusing event organizers of poor communication and mistreatment.

In the letter addressed to the new director of Art Basel Paris, Karim Crippa, the association demanded “concrete proposals for compensating exhibitors," stated that the galleries were never consulted about the event's early closure, and accused organizers of "disrespect, even contempt," according to Monopol. Along with CPGA President and Mon Charpentier gallery co-founder Philippe Charpentier, 14 members of the board signed the letter in support. The day after the association issued the letter, Crippa reportedly wrote to exhibitors promising a "concrete update in the coming days."

On October 22, event organizers for Art Basel Paris emailed exhibitors announcing that "in light of potential demonstrations across Paris this weekend and in the interest of safeguarding our visitors," the fair would close two days ahead of its planned October 25 end date. Following a temporary lockdown during installation at the Grand Palais on October 17, organizers proceeded with the original program before agreeing to end the fair early, citing the ongoing rallies over France’s failing education system and public services that have swept across the nation since mid-September.

#9169. “The Man I Love” Wants Us to Do More Than Mourn

Ira Sachs resists the attention economy, using objects and people to tell a moving story of 1980s New York amid the HIV/AIDS crisis.

In a scene that might be this century’s most faithful depiction of 1980s bohemian New York, a ragtag ensemble crowds around a cluttered dining room table. A mishmash of stemware gleams below the revelers, each importuned to perform a few bars of a song. One self-consciously croons “Someone’s in the Kitchen with Dinah,” another vibratos a Jehovah’s Witness spiritual, while yet another gamely stumbles through the verses of “How Are Things in Glocca Morra?” from Finian’s Rainbow (1968). As gloriously languid as it is insistently idiosyncratic, the tableau readily summons nostalgia for those who remember and those who do not alike. There are no screens; there are no smartphones. There are instead people singing — shyly, joyfully — as though sharing the secret to the universe.

And they are singing, knowing full well that some in the room might not last the year.

A cinematic elegy that urges you to live, Ira Sachs’s The Man I Love is an AIDS movie that isn’t — a movie set in the thick of the pandemic that not only never mentions the illness by name, but entirely dodges the genre’s clichés: no lesion reveal, no tidy redemption, no funeral filled with festive friends. Instead, the film enjoins us to embrace the vitality of the era so as to more potently suffer its imminent loss.

The Man I Love follows “theatre artist” Jimmy George (Rami Malek), a veteran of a downtown performance troupe, as he co-writes a new production and becomes enamored of a young Englishman named Vincent (Luther Ford) who moves into the downstairs unit of their weathered prewar building. Jimmy’s partner Dennis (Tom Sturridge) tolerates the burgeoning affair, but is duly irked by Vincent’s awkward attempts to ingratiate himself into their extensive queer network.

#9168. 10 Art Shows to See in Upstate New York This November

Julia Whitney Barnes’s organic paradise, Emily Nomer’s mystical geometric paintings, Maria Molteni’s conversations with the divine, and more

As autumn unfolds across the East Coast, people around the United States are visiting the polls. May we strip the monsters of power and steer this nation out of its ghoulish ambiance and toward soulful care, not continued scare. In step with the changing times, a robust round of exhibitions in Upstate New York invites you to experience the treats of the season. At Ipso Facto Gallery in Hudson, artists explore creative modalities for surviving the technological hellscape of contemporary life, while Public Private Gallery presents outrageous sculptural works by legendary artists Judy Pfaff and Michael David. Ann Street Gallery features dynamic works by the three artists chosen for their 2026 Emerging Artist Fellowship, and Tyte Gallery showcases a series of lush botanical works on paper by Julia Whitney Barnes. Geometrically inspired paintings by Emily Nomer at Gallery 40 yield bright mystical visions, while a group show at Yellow Studio Arts Center celebrates the commonplace as muse. To all those who fear these hellish times, no more tricks! We conjure our determination and perseverance in the face of ghastly evil!

Ipso Facto Gallery, 362 ½ Warren Street, Hudson, New YorkThrough November 22

Remember life before the internet and obsessive screen time? The TV Glow Sees Me presents the work of five artists who consider how to find themselves amid the “technological hellscape of rapid expansion,” as curator Hannah Studnick puts it in the press release. Featuring mixed-media artworks that reflect a digital culture overflowing with miscellaneous mayhem, Jesse Morsberger’s painting “Up Late” (2026) is a faithful embodiment of our current society: A boy sits alone in a dark room facing the eerie glow of an empty screen. In a crimson-hued scene by Mina Watanabe DeVore, “Look Up” (2026), two youthful figures take a selfie in a graffiti-laden bathroom reminiscent of the legendary Manhattan music club CBGB. Other highlights include Jackson Daughety’s “Where is MrBeast When You Need Him” (2023), a gestural abstract work on stitched canvas, and Allyson Packer’s “Subtropolis 02” (2025), a mash-up sculptural work that includes an LED tube behind a sublimation print in which braces-heavy mouths above a car smash into an unknown object in a bizarre vision that defies explanation.

#9167. 10 Art Books to Curl Up With This November

Celia Paul’s latest essay collection from Venice, Salman Toor’s painted worlds, the secret herbarium of Rosa Luxemburg, a new Roy Lichtenstein catalog for old fans, and more.

The publishing industry is already preparing for spring, but we're still stuck on all the delights and challenges of this fall's slate of art books. Editor-in-Chief Hakim Bishara recommends an exploration of Marxist revolutionary Rosa Luxemburg's secret garden of pressed plants, an art form in its own right; critic Natalie Weis sinks into painter Celia Paul's kinetic prose. Catalogs on Salman Toor, Roy Lichtenstein, and more to discover below. —Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor

Roy Lichtenstein: Like New, edited by Alex Da Corte and Meg Onli | Whitney Museum of American Art, November 3

In this publication, the Whitney frames its Roy Lichtenstein show as a “radical” picture as “never before,” made up of a “novel” selection that is “genuinely new” to an audience “newer than ever” (emphasis the museum’s). But the catalog, inspired by the composition notebooks the artist kept to gather inspirational clippings, doesn’t feel academic or overstuffed, and includes beautiful plates — in other words, it’s easy, clean, and classic, all the reasons we’ve always loved Lichtenstein. —Lisa Yin Zhang

Objects of Desire: An Artist in Venice by Celia Paul | New York Review Books, November 17

Celia Paul writes much like she paints, excavating shimmering insights from familiar subjects, in prose that is as haunting and luminous as her portraits. In this memoir, she uses a Venetian residency to examine her relationship with her deceased husband, mother, and first lover (the unnamed Lucian Freud). Grief, guilt, death, and desire stalk the artist through the city’s narrow corridors; once more, Paul seeks self-knowledge through art, literature, and the act of painting. —Natalie Weis

Visualizing Latinx: Creative Practices in Fashion, Film, and Beyond by Arlene Dávila | Duke University Press, October 13

Arlene Dávila begins where most mainstream criticism of Latinx art ends: by challenging the term itself. The professor and curator’s ninth book continues her decades-long critiques of perfunctory “Latinx representation” through shrewd essays on indie filmmakers, fashion designers, and artists — such as Edra Soto and Ela Troyano — who refuse the tropes imposed on their work and often operate outside of the Los Angeles and New York bubbles. Her insights are a reminder to question the narratives that “make Latinx culture palatable for mainstream culture,” to always dig deeper. —Lakshmi Rivera Amin

Issues touching on arts funding, censorship, AI regulation, and more are at stake for the country’s cultural sectors across key Senate, House, and Gubernatorial races.

Midterms are tomorrow, marking the first nationwide election since President Donald Trump started his second term in the Oval Office. In the wake of Trump’s financial and ideological crackdowns on Smithsonian, unapproved pet projects around the US Capitol, devastation to cultural landscapes through border construction, and dozens of other policies targeting history and heritage, many will be lining up at the polls with arts and culture policies on their minds.

Because Congress ultimately decides appropriations for federal arts entities, such as the National Endowment for the Arts, control of the House and Senate is incredibly important for the cultural sector. (Republicans currently have narrow majorities in both chambers.) From artists running for Congress, like Claire Valdez in New York and musician Bobby Pulido in Texas, to longtime culture advocates like Angie Nixon in the Senate race, we zeroed in on some of the key campaigns to watch in the United States if you care about artistic freedom, affordability for artists, and cultural funding.

We've organized this guide into three sections: Senate, House, and Gubernatorial races. Click through each section below.

Rebecca Schiffman and Lisa Yin Zhang also contributed to this guide.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed leads Republican Mike Rogers by an average of five points in one of this election cycle’s most-anticipated races. El-Sayed, an epidemiologist and the former head of the Detroit and Wayne County health departments, has been subject to repeated racism and culture war tirades over his Muslim faith and criticism of Israel by Rogers and President Trump throughout his campaign. Rogers, a former FBI agent and United States Representative, was endorsed by Trump in July 2025 and has received major funding from pro-Israel lobbying groups during this election cycle.

Elegoo’s Centauri Carbon 2 makes easy four-colour printing affordable – and it's on sale for early Black Friday.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Multicolour 3D printing used to be an expensive business. But that’s changing. Several firms are bringing out capable budget models, and the latest to impress us is the Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2.

Our reviewer, who’s tested many of the best 3D printers over the last decade, found it easy to use, beautifully built and capable of some of the smoothest results he’s had from an FDM machine.

Even at full price, it’s cheaper than the Creality K2 Pro. Now Amazon has dropped it from $424.97 to $401.28, a small yet significant saving.

This enclosed CoreXY printer can take up to four spools at once, making multicolour prints simple to set up. It calibrates itself, handles a wide range of filaments and delivers sharp, consistent results.

Our favourite feature is the Canvas system, which lets you load up to four reels of filament. Our reviewer found it all very quick and easy to load. If your spool has an RFID chip, you just hold it up to the side of the unit and the printer sets everything automatically. When you open a multicolour file, a setup window lets you choose which spool goes where.

The Centauri Carbon 2 uses a CoreXY design for printing speeds of up to 500mm per second, with a respectable 256 x 256 x 256mm build volume. Our reviewer printed a one-piece fidget toy with moving parts, which came out silky smooth.

The main drawback is size: with the spools on the side and a waste chute at the back, you’ll need plenty of space around it. Otherwise, this a great value, especially at this discounted price. Read our full Elegoo Centauri Carbon 2 review for more details.

#9164. Russia’s security service detains teen over alleged terror plot targeting Moscow museum

The Tsaritsyno palace in Moscow Photo courtesy the office of the mayor of Moscow, via Wikimedia Commons

Russia’s FSB security service has detained a teenager on charges of threatening Moscow’s Tsaritsyno Museum and Nature Reserve via TikTok after an unusual warning from US officials of a “credible threat of a mass casualty event” on 31 October. The alert was posted on the website of the US embassy in Moscow and social media. Der Spiegel reported that German citizens in Russia had received a similar warning.

On 1 November, the FSB distributed a video, published on sites such as Tass, the official state news agency, showing an unidentified young man being detained, footage of a knife, camouflage and neo-Nazi content on his phone, and his confession to posting “propaganda of Nazism” on his TikTok page. Russia’s National Antiterrorism Committee posted the same footage to its YouTube channel.

The US issued a similar alert several days before an attack that killed at least 149 people in March 2024 during a concert at Crocus City Hall in Moscow. Islamic State claimed responsibility for the attack; before it occurred, Russian President Vladimir Putin denounced the warnings as “outright blackmail”.

In a change reflecting US President Donald Trump’s cooperation with Russia, the FSB in a statement on 1 November, posted on the agency’s website, credited “US law enforcement agencies” for warning of an impending attack at Tsaritsyno: “We are grateful to the American side for the information provided.”

The FSB statement added that “in the interest of public safety, planned cultural events at the museum-reserve have been cancelled, and security measures in the surrounding area have been stepped up”. The museum is typically closed on Mondays, while the surrounding park, known for its rolling hills, fountains and wooded paths, is open daily. Russian media reported that the park reopened on Sunday.

The FSB’s statement claims the detained minor had posted images on TikTok “showing himself wearing tactical gear—including a balaclava, cap, eyewear and headset—while holding an object resembling an automatic weapon” as well as “photographs taken at the Tsaritsyno Museum-Reserve, accompanied by the caption: ‘I found a place’”.

The complex, which was originally intended as a summer residence for Catherine the Great in the 18th century, is consistently ranked as one of Moscow’s most visited tourist sites. Tsaritsyno’s website states that over 7 million people visit the museum and park in southern Moscow annually. The Grand Palace, its centrepiece, is known for its neo-Gothic design by the architect Matvey Kazakov, which remained unfinished after Catherine’s death. Many other buildings on the grounds were designed by Kazakov’s teacher, Vasily Bazhenov, Catherine’s court architect, who was initially commissioned to design the palace before falling out with the Empress.

Some preservationists denounced the glitzy completion of the palace, inaugurated in 2007 with Putin present. It was carried out under Moscow’s mayor at the time, Yury Luzhkov, who was known for monumental construction projects. Although some attempts have been made to show contemporary art at Tsaritsyno, its exhibitions are primarily focused on the tsars and historic Russian folk crafts.

As the Moscow institution is temporarily closed and its director, Roman Romanov, is dismissed, fears grow that Russia’s past is being glossed over

Landmark site was the burial place of Prince Grigory Potemkin, whose bones were removed by Russian occupying forces last year

The Pushkin design satellite will have both historic and contemporary design galleries

Zelfira Tregulova, who has headed the State Tretyakov Gallery since 2015, will be replaced by Elena Pronicheva, who has links to Vladimir Putin

#9163. Henry Holland creates wallpaper and fabric collection with a "language developed through ceramics"

Designer Henry Holland‘s textual fabric and textile collection for luxury interior furnishings company Harlequin was informed by his work as a ceramicist, he tells Dezeen in this interview.

Simply named Harlequin x Henry Holland, the collection of wallpapers and fabrics was heavily influenced by both the extensive archive of Harlequin’s parent company Sanderson and Holland’s love of the Japanese pottery technique nerikomi.

“The starting point for the collection was our ceramic work,” Holland told Dezeen. “We used the organic patterns and forms created in our handbuilt work as the starting point, and then similarly we built the colour palettes around the clays that we use to create our pieces.”

“To add further depth and range to the collection, we also delved into the incredibly rich archive that the Sanderson group have across all of their brands and reinterpreted some archive prints that felt like the right additions to the collection.”

The collection features four distinct fabrics that translate ceramic patterns and colours into materials that can transform interior spaces.

For Holland, this transformation of scale, from a hand-held object to entire rooms and interiors, was the most exciting part of the collaboration.

“For me, the collection is really about taking the language we have developed through ceramics and allowing it to live on a completely different scale,” he said.

“At the studio we make objects that sit within a room, whereas with Harlequin we suddenly had the opportunity to take those patterns, colours and textures and make them become the room,” he added.

“There is something really exciting about that shift in perspective. Our work has always been about balancing the graphic with the organic, and I think that really comes through in the collection. There are moments that feel bold and energetic and others that are much softer and quieter.”

Holland worked closely with the Harlequin team to understand which elements of the nerikomi technique could be translated and upscaled to fabric. He found clear similarities in methodology between the technique and the process of making textile fabrics.

“With nerikomi, the pattern isn’t something that is applied to the surface afterwards – it is created through the material itself by layering, compressing, slicing and rebuilding different coloured clays,” he said. “There is always this balance between control and chance, which is something I love about the process.”

“Working with the Harlequin team and looking at those surfaces and identifying elements within them that could become a wallpaper or a fabric was fascinating,” he continued.

“We were able to isolate gestures, enlarge details and play with scale in ways I wouldn’t necessarily have considered. Some tiny detail from a ceramic piece can suddenly become this huge, immersive pattern across a wall.”

Holland has a personal connection to each of the four fabrics developed for the collection – Southborough, Elsworthy, Great Hey and Blenets Check Mini – and each was named after one of his and his partner’s former homes.

“We created a really autobiographical narrative by naming the patterns and pieces in the collection after homes that my husband and I have lived in through our lives,” he said.

While the patterning on the fabrics, which ranges from checkerboard in Blenets Check Mini to moiré-style in Elsworthy and chevrons in Southborough, was informed by ceramics, so too were the colours selected.

Pastel tones of chocolate and moss were informed by unglazed pottery, while Holland looked to glazed earthenware for the collection’s bolder colours.

“We were able to split the palette into more subdued, almost pastel tones, taking our lead from our unglazed ceramics, and then a bolder level of colour where we used our glazed pieces as the reference,” explained Holland.

“It was really important to me that, even though we were translating the work into completely different materials and applications, everything still felt very rooted in the studio and recognisably ours.”

Although the fabrics and wallpapers in the collection each have a distinct aesthetic and feel, Holland believes the pieces form a coherent collection because they come from a shared creative thought process.

“They share a common DNA because ultimately they all come back to the same source material, which is the ceramics,” he said.

“Within my ceramic work there has always been a contrast between very precise pattern and much looser, more organic pattern. Some pieces can be incredibly controlled and almost mathematical, while others are much more fluid. I didn’t want to lose that contrast when translating the work into print,” he continued.

“What brings everything together is colour, movement and the sense that everything has been touched by hand. Even when the patterns are quite different, there is a shared irregularity and energy to them. Nothing feels too perfect or overly digital, and that was really important to me.”

Holland hopes designers will use the collection’s fabrics in a wide variety of interiors, working out how to combine and layer pieces to create unique and interesting spaces.

“I don’t think there should be too many rules around how it is used,” he said. “One of the things we really wanted was for the collection to have enough cohesion that you could layer different elements together without everything having to match perfectly.”

“The colour stories run throughout the collection, so you can pick up a tone from one of the more expressive wallpapers and echo it through a fabric or a quieter pattern elsewhere in the room,” continued Holland. “I think interiors are much more interesting when there is that kind of tension.”

Overall, Holland hopes people will enjoy using the fabrics and wallpapers and enjoy the spaces that are created.

“Ultimately, I want people to have fun with it,” he said. “I like interiors that feel collected and personal rather than overly prescribed.”

“Hopefully the collection gives designers and customers the tools to create spaces that have personality, warmth and a real sense of individuality,” he continued.

The collection is the result of a deep collaboration between Holland and Harlequin, which has resulted in its success.

“It was a very genuine back-and-forth process,” said Holland. “I didn’t want to simply hand over some ceramic patterns and say, ‘turn these into wallpaper’.”

“The interesting part was bringing together what we know about ceramics and pattern at Henry Holland Studio with Harlequin’s incredible knowledge of textiles, wallpaper, colour and interiors,” he continued.

“We started with the ceramics and the archive of patterns and colour combinations we have developed at the studio, and from there the Harlequin team began exploring scale, repeats, textures and different interpretations. We would respond to those, push certain things further, pull other things back and keep refining the palette.”

Holland believes this close collaboration is key to the collection’s success.

“I think the best collaborations happen when both sides bring something to the project that the other couldn’t necessarily achieve alone,” he said.

“There are things in this collection that feel Henry Holland Studio completely, but they have been transformed through Harlequin’s expertise into something entirely new. That’s what made the whole process so rewarding.”

Not every side hustle is created equal. Some trade your time for minimal pay. Others leverage skills you already have and can scale into serious income streams. The FI community has tested all of these, and the ones that consistently accelerate financial independence share two traits: they pay well relative to time invested, and they build skills or assets that increase in value over time.

The table below covers 15 proven methods organized by income potential. Focus on the ones that match your existing skills — the learning curve is shorter and you start earning faster.

From the FI perspective, even $1,000 per month in side income — invested consistently at 7% annual returns — grows to over $520,000 in 20 years. That is a meaningful chunk of most people's FI number generated entirely outside their day job.

The highest-paying way to earn extra money from home is freelancing skills you already use in your career. A marketing manager can freelance marketing strategy at $75-$150 per hour. An accountant can do bookkeeping for small businesses at $40-$80 per hour. A software developer can build features for startups at $100-$200 per hour.

The reason this works so well is that you skip the learning curve entirely. You already have the expertise — you just need clients. Start by telling your professional network you are available for freelance work, update your LinkedIn headline, and join industry-specific Slack communities where potential clients post projects.

The internet is flooded with "make $10,000 per month from your couch" claims. Most of them are selling you a course, not showing you a realistic business model. The FI community values honesty about what works, what the realistic ramp-up time looks like, and what red flags signal a scam.

Extra income does not just pad your bank account — it fundamentally changes the math of financial independence. The FI community has identified side income as one of the most powerful levers because it directly increases your savings rate without requiring you to cut spending.

Consider a household earning $80,000 with a 30% savings rate. They save $24,000 per year and reach FI in approximately 28 years. Now add $1,500 per month in side income ($18,000 per year) with all of it invested:

That $1,500 per month in side income — invested consistently — cuts nine years off your FI timeline. Nine years of freedom purchased by working an extra 10-15 hours per week for a period, then potentially scaling back once the compounding takes hold.

Self-employment income above $400 per year triggers self-employment tax (15.3% for Social Security and Medicare) on top of your regular income tax. But self-employment also unlocks powerful tax advantages that the FI community leverages heavily:

A Solo 401(k) funded with side-hustle income is one of the FI community's favorite strategies. Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The FI community has proven that side income is one of the fastest ways to accelerate your path to financial independence. Even $1,000 per month — fully invested at 7% returns — grows to over $520,000 in 20 years. But the real power is in how it transforms your savings rate: moving from 30% to 45% can cut nearly a decade off your FI date. Focus on scalable skills, invest every extra dollar, and use self-employment tax advantages like the Solo 401(k) to maximize the impact.

A practical roadmap from zero to first dollar.

List every professional skill you use at work — writing, design, analysis, project management, coding, teaching. The skills your employer pays you for are the same skills clients will pay for.

Pro tip: Ask three colleagues what they think you do best. External perspective reveals strengths you take for granted.

Do not try five things at once. Pick the method that matches your strongest skill and start on one platform. Freelancing on Upwork, tutoring on Wyzant, or selling on Etsy — focus beats diversification at the start.

Create 2-3 samples that showcase your work. For freelancing, this might be writing samples or design mockups. For consulting, a one-page overview of your expertise and results you have achieved.

Start with your network — friends, former colleagues, LinkedIn connections. Offer an introductory rate to build testimonials and case studies. Your first three clients prove the concept and generate referrals.

Pro tip: Price your introductory rate at 70-80% of your target rate, not 50%. Underpricing signals low quality.

Open a separate bank account for side income. Automatically transfer 30% to a tax savings account and invest the rest in index funds or your Solo 401(k).

Pro tip: Set aside money for quarterly estimated tax payments to avoid penalties.

Most people earn $500-$2,000 per month within 3-6 months of consistent effort. Freelancers with professional skills can earn $2,000-$5,000+ per month once established. The income depends on your skills, time investment, and chosen method — but $500-$1,000 per month is achievable for almost anyone willing to put in 10-15 hours per week.

Freelancing skills you already have is the fastest path. If you can write, design, code, manage projects, or do bookkeeping — you can find your first client within 1-2 weeks through your existing professional network or platforms like Upwork. Selling unused items on eBay or Facebook Marketplace generates cash within days.

Yes. Any self-employment income over $400 per year must be reported. You will owe self-employment tax (15.3%) plus your regular income tax rate. However, you can deduct business expenses and contribute to a Solo 401(k) or SEP IRA to significantly reduce your tax burden. Set aside 25-30% of side income for taxes.

Yes, but check your employment contract for non-compete or moonlighting clauses. Most employers have no issue with side work that does not compete directly with their business. Use evenings and weekends to build your side income, and never use your employer's equipment or time for side projects.

Avoid anything that requires upfront payment, promises guaranteed income, involves recruiting others to earn (MLM), or has vague job descriptions. Legitimate opportunities clearly state what you will do, how you will be paid, and do not require you to invest money to start. If it sounds too good to be true, it is.

Extra income is one of the most powerful FI accelerators. An extra $1,000 per month invested at 7% returns grows to $520,000+ in 20 years. More importantly, it increases your savings rate without requiring spending cuts. Moving from a 30% to 45% savings rate can cut nearly a decade off your FI timeline.

Making extra money from home is not about finding a magic solution — it is about leveraging skills you already have and investing the earnings strategically. Start with one method that matches your strongest skill, land your first three clients through your network, and invest every extra dollar toward financial independence. The FI community has shown that even $1,000 per month in side income can cut years off your timeline and add hundreds of thousands to your net worth. The key is starting today and staying consistent.

#9160. EU Looking to Downgrade Money Laundering Risk in Art and Antiquities Trade

The European Commission, the executive branch of the European Union, is planning to downgrade its assessment of the money laundering and terrorist financing threat posed by the art trade, the Financial Times reports.

While a Commission spokesperson told the FT that the risk assessment has not yet been finalized, the paper pointed to publicly available minutes from a January 29, 2026, meeting in Brussels of the Commission’s Expert Sub-Group on Dialogue with the Art Market.

At that meeting, the Directorate-General for Financial Stability, Financial Services and Capital Markets Union (DG FISMA), which is responsible for EU banking and finance policy, presented key findings from its upcoming 2026 Supranational Risk Assessment (SNRA) on money laundering and terrorist financing. The minutes say the report will be published in 2026. The new assessment rates the threat linked to works of art and antiques as “moderate” (level 2), a downgrade from the previous assessment in 2022, which rated it as “high,” citing “limited EU evidence.” Related Articles Connecticut Antiques Dealer Pleads Guilty in $2.1 M. Theft Scheme Gagosian Succession Plan, Rembrandt Masterpiece May Contain Copied Dog, Money Laundering Rises in UK Art Market, and More: Morning Links for September 24, 2025

Alongside the downgrade, DG FISMA put forward a series of recommendations “aimed at mitigating risks and strengthening regulatory oversight” of the art trade. These include “continuous dialogue with stakeholders in the art and antiques markets, alongside awareness-raising campaigns, targeted training programmes, and the development of guidance and codes of ethics to promote compliance and best practices.”

The British Art and Design Association, according to the minutes, “welcomed the reassessment,” while the antiquities-focused industry group, the International Association of Dealers in Ancient Art, challenged even the moderate risk assesement, pointing to reports by the European Commission’s Financial Intelligence Unit, which found that only 0.3 percent of art and antiquities items in the EU have been connected to criminal cases.

#9159. Foster + Partners unveils replacement for landmark San Siro stadium in Milan

British architecture studio Foster + Partners and US studio Manica have unveiled their design for Generali Stadium, a new football stadium for clubs AC Milan and Inter Milan, set to replace Italy’s iconic San Siro.

Planned to be built alongside the 99-year-old San Siro stadium, which will later be torn down, the 71,500-seat replacement will be defined by a structural facade composed of elongated X-framed concrete supports.

Foster + Partners‘ founder Norman Foster told Dezeen the overarching goal is “to create a new home for two storied football clubs, which captures the unique energy of the city and its distinctive architectural and structural traditions”.

“The Generali Stadium celebrates the enduring connection between the football clubs – FC Internazionale Milano (Inter Milan) and AC Milan – and the city of Milano and will drive this shared heritage into the future,” he explained.

The design reveal follows the sale of the iconic stadium to the two rival football teams, which was approved by Milan’s city council in October 2025. It is being developed by Foster’s firm with the US practice Manica, and the naming rights belong to insurance giant Generali.

AC Milan and Inter Milan will continue to share the existing San Siro venue until the 2032 European Championship, co-hosted by Italy, for which the new stadium is scheduled to be completed. San Siro will then be demolished, according to the BBC.

Generali Stadium’s defining feature is its pre-cast structural facade, which will support the stadium bowl and double-curved roof. This will also frame and naturally ventilate a series of lofty loggia-like spaces on its upper levels, intended to feel open and welcoming.

“The structural facade is the defining architectural concept of the stadium: a holistic and monumental piece of infrastructure rising approximately 60 metres in height, composed of interlocking low-carbon precast concrete segments connected through expressed structural joints,” Foster said.

“It is a celebration of Milanese and Italian engineering tradition, where architecture and structure become one,” Foster explained.

Another distinctive element will be “two curvas” – the curved north and south stands, designed to bring spectators near to the pitch, with opposing fans closely facing each other.

“That relationship of two opposing walls of supporters, each tied to one of the city’s great clubs, is unique to Milan and found in no other stadium in the world,” said Manica founder David Manica.

“The whole seating bowl is built around it,” he told Dezeen. “Rather than starting with an image or an icon, we began with the experience of the fans. The architecture is a result of that guiding principle.”

According to Foster, this design also draws on San Siro’s distinctive structure.

“Its seating bowl is inspired by the San Siro itself, with its distinctive ‘curvas’, but with greater proximity to the pitch,” Foster explained.

“The external shape is driven by the curvas behind the goals. Here, the north and south ends rise on a 37-degree pitch to house 11,700 at each end – north for Internazionale and south for AC Milan.”

The stadium is planned to be all-electric and carbon-neutral in operation, targeting LEED Gold Certification. The roof will incorporate 27,500 square metres of photovoltaic panels, while a “low-carbon precast concrete system” will be utilised to minimise waste and construction time.

The bowl’s geometry will be engineered to “amplify the roar of crowds within the stadium, enhancing the atmosphere during events while significantly reducing acoustic spillover and noise pollution”, Foster said.

“San Siro is famous for its noise, and the best way to honour that legacy was to capture that atmosphere – and amplify it,” added David Manica.

“We treated acoustics as a primary design driver from the very first sketches,” he said. “The result is a stadium where the chanting and singing build on themselves, taking the atmosphere Milanese supporters love and making it even more powerful.”

The project forms part of a wider 281,000-square-metre masterplan that will combine public spaces with green areas and leisure and retail zones.

Designed by architect Ulisse Stacchini, San Siro, otherwise known as Stadio Giuseppe Meazza, was built in 1925. It has been modified several times over its lifetime, but has remained unchanged since the 1990 World Cup.

The possibility of its demolition emerged in 2019, when AC Milan and Inter Milan announced they were exploring plans to build a replacement venue for San Siro.

The clubs later selected a design by architecture studio Populous, called the Cathedral, but the Regional Commission for the Cultural Heritage of Lombardy blocked its development in 2023 because of the existing building’s cultural significance.

Demolition was made possible by the building’s sale, which was approved after an overnight debate that took place for nearly 12 hours.

At the time, mayor Giuseppe Sala suggested the sale would prevent Milan from being left “with the burden of an abandoned arena”, as the two clubs had begun exploring plans to build two separate stadiums on the city’s outskirts.

Reflecting on the project, Foster said the Generali Stadium’s design draws on his “great personal connection with the city”.

“As a student of architecture, I spent many hours walking through and sketching its heroic public spaces – the urban route of the historic Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II and individual structures such as the Torre Velasca and Pirelli Tower – and studying the pioneering work of Pier Luigi Nervi,” he explained.

“The verticality and rhythm of the Duomo, the civic generosity of the city’s porticos, and the spatial experience of the city’s great public plazas have all been inspirational and inseparable as a background to the design of the Generali Stadium, which will be a new civic monument for Milano.”

Elsewhere, Foster + Partners is also developing its design for Manchester United’s new 100,000-seat stadium in the UK.

The stadium, which is designed with a giant tent-like structure, was described by Foster as “one of the most exciting projects in the world”.

#9157. Hard Truths: Should a Jilted Artist Keep Applying for Grants?

With a world in crisis and an art market spinning out of control, ace art-world consultants Chen & Lampert deliver hard truths in response to questions sent by Art in America readers from far and wide.

Last year you answered a reader’s question about grants, and it really got me thinking. I’m a mid-career artist with 25 years of exhibitions in respected galleries and art spaces. I never pursued grants or residencies earlier in my career, and as a result my credentials might appear thin. Your response prompted me to apply for a number of different grants, but so far nothing has worked out. Doing all this paperwork is actually pretty depressing. I feel like I gave it a go and should move on, but there’s a part of me that wants to keep at it despite my low chances. Is it worth it to keep trying? Related Articles Hard Choices: Is Our Advice Helpful? Hard Truths: Can Senior Citizens Be Sage Social-Media Ambassadors?

Once you’ve double-checked the project budget and resized JPEGs to the required DPI, your anxiety and acid reflux start acting up as you wonder: What if my application is declined? How will I make my work without a grant? At this point you’ve held steady for a quarter-century and managed to survive without hard-earned handouts. It appears that what you really desire is support, by which we mean acknowledgement from peers, panelists, and the extended Guggenheim family. But also, of course, a comically oversized check that can actually be deposited in a real FDIC-insured bank.

There is no shake-and-bake recipe for getting a grant, aside from the not-so-secret herbs and spices that are nepotism and cronyism. Lacking these ingredients, you still need to fry up a concise application that thoughtfully demonstrates the timeliness and urgency of your proposed project. Make sure to emphasize your decades of experience and demonstrate how grant-givers’ support will substantially bolster your vision at this crucial juncture. Don’t focus on dates, names, or details listed on the attached CV; instead, gush to them about compelling new ideas and your enthusiasm for building on previous accomplishments. They’d have to be cretinous schmucks not to want to help you grow.

You may opt to give up … or you could keep sending in the same, lightly touched-up application every grant season. Chances are they’ll eventually be forced to acknowledge you. This probably sounds outlandish, but we know rejectees who’ve doggedly hounded the same foundations for years and years until finally nabbing their award. If you think this is obnoxious and demeaning, remember that many of our most visible and rewarded artists are also our most tenacious naggers. Major funding organizations essentially recognize that you won’t stop applying, and whether they truly believe in your mission, they may ultimately greenlight a grant to make you go far, far away.

I work in the storage area at a gallery and while reshelving things I dropped a painting. No one saw it happen. The piece was wrapped with foam, but a corner got dinged. The art is just going back on the rack for the time being, so do I have to tell my boss? They’ll discover it eventually, but by then I won’t be working here anymore.

Here’s how we suspect this will go: It may be weeks, months or even years, but the discoverer of the damaged painting won’t care enough to investigate what happened. Sure, the gallerist will be miffed, but what’s new about that? An art handler (who, like you, won’t last long) will deliver the canvas to a framer for repair or replacement. They’ll charge a small fortune, but that’s par for the course because the bill—along with charges for the opening dinner, the e-flux ad, bubble wrap, and all other operational costs the gallery can tack on—will all be deducted from the artist’s cut of the sale. Or, just as likely, the piece will continue collecting dust until doomsday. By that point you’ll have far more pressing things to attend to, like finding potable water and not getting mowed down by bloodthirsty Waymo cabs. The karmic butterfly effect of one busted frame is nothing to fret about considering what’s coming.

#9156. traditional bamboo scaffolding and tea-waste panels shape impromptu projects’ pagoda in macau

referencing traditional pagoda forms, the temporary installation integrates a slender bamboo frame and translucent fabric skin along macau's shoreline.

Joao O edited by christina vergopoulou November 1, 2026 3 min

Sited on the shoreline of Sai Van Lake in Macau, Bamboo Pagoda is a 13-meter-tall temporary pavilion designed by local practice Impromptu Projects, led by Rita Machado and João Ó. The installation draws directly from Macau’s vernacular bamboo scaffolding, a building technique listed on the city’s Inventory of Intangible Cultural Heritage in 2017, reinterpreting construction-grade craft into a contemporary waterfront pavilion for contemplation.

The design by Impromptu Projects studio references classical pagoda geometries and Taoist concepts of equilibrium, structured over an octagonal footprint that tapers as it ascends. Slender structural bamboo culms form the exposed load-bearing skeleton, bound using traditional scaffolding lashing methods. A semi-translucent skin of bamboo fabric wraps the framework, filtering natural light and diffusing the vertical profile. Grounding the structure, the floor surface is laid with composite panels manufactured by Macau-based firm Zence Object Technology (CHAZENCE), composed of recycled tea waste and discarded wood chips. Integrated solar panels power the project’s architectural spotlights off the municipal grid, combining intangible cultural heritage with circular material systems.
