A burger chain's pixel-art RPG has gamers excited, and there are good reasons for that.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If you’d told me a decade ago that Wendy's would release one of the most talked-about indie RPGs of 2026, I’d have assumed your burger had some dodgy mushrooms. Yet here we are: it's actually happening.

The world's third-largest hamburger fast-food chain has unveiled a turn-based, pixel-art adventure in which its red-haired mascot leads a party of fast-food heroes to save a kingdom in peril. It's called WendyQuest: Legend of the Four Corner Stones. No, this is not a South Park parody. This is a real, playable game.

The branded element isn't just about bigging up Wendy's either: it also takes potshots at rivals. In the game, for example, your enemies include Frydusa, a carton of snake-like French fries, and a gang called the Golden Archers. As a dig at McDonald’s, it's not subtle.

81monkeys, an indie studio in Port Moody, British Columbia, is making the game, and it’s heading to Steam. You might expect something so obviously corporate to either get trounced on social media or get ignored and sink without a trace. At the time of writing, though, gamers mostly seem to be asking… why it looks so good.

There's more. Last summer, Pepsi asked on social media whether it should make a video game. It was buried in replies pointing out that it already had. One came from Kotaro Uchikoshi, now a celebrated visual-novel director (yes, that's a thing now), who'd worked on 1999’s Pepsiman and was offering to reconnect the company with the original team.

Branded games are clearly back on the menu. The question is… why? Well, first it's worth noting that we've been here before.

Domino’s Avoid the Noid in 1989 is widely cited as the first fast-food tie-in game. McDonald’s followed with Global Gladiators, which is considered one of the best platformers of its era. Then there was Cool Spot, starring the red dot from 7 Up’s American logo, which you could play on the SNES and Mega Drive in 1993 and, branding tie-in aside, is a genuinely brilliant 2D platform game.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

The original Pepsiman, though, remains the king of the branded games. Released only in Japan (which always helps cult status), it showed a superhero sprinting through cities to deliver Pepsi cans. And it remains much-loved: these days, copies go for hundreds of dollars on sites like eBay.

Then came Burger King's 2006 experiment. The chain sold three branded Xbox games for $3.99, including the infamous stealth title Sneak King, as long as you bought a value meal (sold separately). BK ended up shifting more than 3.2 million copies in total.

KFC was late to the party, only joining the fun in 2019 with I Love You, Colonel Sanders! A Finger Lickin’ Good Dating Simulator. The parody dating sim got flayed by critics, but players loved it, giving it a 91% positive rating on Steam.

From a branding perspective, what's interesting is that these weren’t just adverts with gameplay bolted on. They were proper games that people actually liked, even if reviewers were somewhat sniffy. So why are they coming back now? It's difficult to say, but I think a few factors are in play.

First, the original branded games' child audience is now an adult audience with money, and nostalgia is a powerful force. Second, it’s far easier to distribute games today. While Burger King once had to manufacture physical copies and distribute them to restaurants, now Wendy’s just needs a Steam page.

Thirdly, traditional advertising is struggling to break through ad blockers, ad-free subscriptions and a general lack of interest. In contrast, people actually like a branded game. They might even actively seek it out.

Finally, there's the backlash against AI. Wendy's Steam page proudly declares its game “100% fresh and 100% human-made” for a reason. As we all drown in AI slop, handcrafted, indie-style pixel art becomes a visual statement of brand values.

None of this, of course, guarantees that these games will succeed. For every Global Gladiators there’s a Sneak King, a game remembered more as a curio than for its gameplay. The brands that get this right treat players as players, not targets for ads.

So will WendyQuest join Pepsiman in the hall of fame, or end up in the bargain bin of history? I have no clue. But if a burger chain can get me excited about a turn-based RPG, its marketing team must be doing something right. And Pepsi, if you’re reading: Uchikoshi’s offer is still on the table.

Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

#9154. In Fiery Court Filing, Democratic Lawmaker Says Kennedy Center’s Closure Is Meant to Hide Its Failure Under Trump

The much-debated potential two-year closure of the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts is being proposed to cover up the institution’s failings since US president Donald Trump installed loyalists to the board and became its chair, says Ohio Democrat Joyce Beatty in a fiery 51-page Friday filing in US District Court for Washington, D.C. Beatty is an ex-officio member of the board of trustees. Trump has insisted the closure is necessary and dictated a date for it, the filing points out, without any proper board oversight.

The strongly worded filing says the administration has responded “grudgingly—to put it generously” to requests for information; criticizes a defense by Trump as being based on “a fake one-year review that never happened”; cites a “sham process to lend a false patina of legitimacy”; and, in a piquant choice of words given Trump’s admiration of the Russian dictator Vladimir Putin, calls Trump’s decision to close the center a “ukase,” a term referring to a proclamation by a tsar. All that is on page one. Related Articles Former Presidents Obama, Clinton Mock Trump's White House Interiors With Comparisons to 'Saddam Hussein' and 'Liberace's Bathroom' Donors Are Secretly Trying to Save the Kennedy Center's Artworks from 'Destruction' or Disposal Amid Trump Takeover

The Kennedy Center referred ARTnews’s request for comment on the filing to the Department of Justice, which did not immediately respond.

Charles Matthew Floca, facilities manager, was charged with finding a consultant “to bless Trump’s closure decision,” says the filing. Only the Delta Consulting Group applied, and the group was required to provide a recommendation within just days. The board approved Trump’s decision to close the center on August 13, 2025, and, says the filing, only received Delta’s written report on August 31, two weeks later. “The bizarre timeline says it all,” says the filing.

The board then held another vote on September 15, seemingly indicating the insufficiency of the first one, and, says the filing, preparatory materials were provided to participants just three days before. It contained serious inaccuracies, says the filing, including that congressionally appropriated funds for the center’s renovation must be spent by September 2029, which Beatty says is false, pointing out that the funds can be spent through September 2034.

The “kicker,” says the filing, is that Floca and others told trustees that construction costs would double, increasing by more than $300 million, if a phased approach to repairs were implemented. Meanwhile, letters from real estate services company Jones Lang LaSalle, called upon to outline the schedule for renovations, make clear that “Delta’s estimates were exaggerated,” but those letters were not shared with the trustees.

The two-year closure plan, says the filing, “was designed, not in good faith for the best interests of the Center, but to cover up Defendants’ own mismanagement and to please Trump.”

The filing says that the organization’s chief financial officer texted Floca on September 10, saying, “We need to get shut” because “we are burning money,” memorializing statements by the board’s vice chair, Jennifer Fischer, in a conversation with US commerce secretary Howard Lutnick. She also said that “opponents [will] say [prior Kennedy Center president Richard] Grenell raised a ton of money and then we burned it to the ground.”

The timeline, says the filing, is transparently motivated by Trump’s desire to preside over the reopening. As Lutnick himself said outside the courthouse ahead of a hearing, “why would the President agree to work on the restoration where he’s going to be the President for the next… two-and-a-half years, and then he’s leaving?”

Trump fired the longtime board chair in February 2025 and stocked the board with supporters, and was swiftly elected chair by the new board members; Floca was appointed in March 2026 though he “lacks arts management expertise.”

Attendance and donations then dropped significantly. In December 2025, the board announced it would add Trump’s name to the center, a move Beatty sued to stop. Artists canceled scheduled performances and ticket sales dropped by as much as 70 percent, notes the filing. Trump announced on February 1, 2026 that “I have determined” that the center would close on July 4 and cease operations to allow for a two-year renovation, citing a “one year review” with experts. “No such review ever happened,” says Beatty’s filing.

Congress had appropriated $257 million for upkeep of the building in 2025, with construction phased out over time and the center remaining open. Floca initially said he recommended the two-year closure in January 2026, and has testified that the duration was set by Trump in a message on his social media platform, Truth Social. Beatty amended her suit to stop the closure and requested information to evaluate the validity of the decision. Defendants failed to provide information just days before a scheduled March 16 vote, she says, resulting in the court issuing an order requiring defendants to hand over materials. But no such materials had even been prepared, says the filing.

By the time the meeting came, Trump said it was “too late for the board” to object “because we’ve already announced the closure.” Trustee input was, he said, a “minor detail.”

Despite a court ruling prohibiting the closure, management wound down programming, says the filing. Foca claims he took no efforts to develop the 2026–27 season and even encouraged the National Symphony Orchestra to leave the campus, depriving the center of thousands of ticket sales. Staff layoffs continued.

Changing input from JLL, meantime, first indicated that total closure was necessary, but later revised its advice, saying phased renovations were feasible but also noting that the Kennedy Center’s “true needs approach $400–450 million.” Keeping the center open during the work would incur additional costs of $60 million–$80 million. The latter message was withheld from the trustees, says the filing.

The board then looked for a consultant to support the necessity of Trump’s proposed two-year closure. Only Delta Consulting Group applied, though, according to Beatty, it “lacked any expertise in performing arts management.” It was told to assume a two-year closure beginning with Trump’s decreed date of July 6. JLL’s revised assessment, saying the center could remain open during work, was not provided to Delta.

What’s more, documents included in the filing indicate that Lutnick “shaped the content of Delta’s presentation,” which stated that phased renovations would cost some $560 million, more than twice what Congress had appropriated. “Management knew that was not accurate,” says the filing, noting that JLL’s updated plan calculated only an additional cost of $41 million for a phased renovation.

Furthermore, the defendants produced JLL’s second, revised report only after the completion of depositions in the case, despite its relevance, says the filing, adding that Floca denied under questioning that any updated plan existed.

Heavy rains on September 4 caused the collapse of a small section of ceiling plaster in the foyer, which the center informed staff would result in closure for the rest of the day. Three days before the September 15 meeting, the board received new information, containing two draft resolutions. One again proposed adding Trump’s name to the building, saying that “certain fiscal collapse” would result if Trump were not recognized on the building’s facade as he could not be expected to provide oversight without receiving that distinction. “This was the first and only time that the full Board has been informed of the institution’s ‘certain fiscal collapse,’” says the filing. It also proposed once again that the board approve Trump’s plan to close for two years. It revealed for the first time that Delta and Floca considered the main building “unsafe for continued occupancy.”

Beatty appealed to the court and the renaming proposal was taken off the agenda.

Floca then told the trustees that phased work would double the cost, and the board voted for closure. Trump said that day on social media that the center would close immediately but that renovation couldn’t continue until the court ruled on the name change and that if it did not go through, the work would not take place.

Floca then announced on September 16 that the main building would need to close immediately for safety reasons. The same day, Trump told reporters that unless his name went on the facade, “it’s going to close, it will end up being ripped down.” The same night, a photographer captured an image of him on Air Force One, reading a placard that appeared to read “Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED.”

#9153. Lighting design a "strategic economic investment" says Signify's Sameer Sodhi

According to business leader of entertainment and Colour Kinetics at lighting brand Signify, Sameer Sodhi, lit-up architecture and public installations can encourage interaction, strengthen local identity and support overall wellbeing.

Sodhi explained that for decades, the value of a building has been measured by appearance, energy performance, return on investment and construction costs. A building’s lighting design is one of the most influential factors but is often overlooked and seen as a “finishing touch”.

He added that well-designed lighting can shape the experience of places, support local economies and strengthen communities.

“The question is no longer whether lighting matters,” Sodhi said. “But whether we can accurately measure the (overlooked) value it creates.”

Sodhi points to a recent study by lighting brand Colour Kinetics that examined four illuminated spaces across the United States and found that lighting generated social, economic, and cultural benefits “well beyond the initial investment”.

“The report assesses lighting through a broader framework that includes community engagement, tourism, economic development, media visibility, partnerships, sustainability and health and wellbeing,” Sodhi explained.

“Rather than viewing lighting as an isolated building system, it recognised it as infrastructure capable of influencing how cities function and how communities connect,” he added.

Sodhi cites the lighting of Daniel Hoan Memorial Bridge in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, as an example, which has transformed the infrastructure into a “dynamic visual icon” that reflects the city’s identity and connects residents and visitors to the waterfront.

“The bridge now hosts community and civic events, causes and initiatives and annual festivals, while serving as a canvas for civic celebrations throughout the year,” he said.

According to Sodhi, architectural lighting also creates economic value. For example, the thoughtful lighting design of West Sacramento’s Barns in California has supported the area’s placemaking.

Although the venue was originally conceived as an event and dining venue, the strategic lighting design has helped establish it as the focal point for the surrounding mixed-use district, which includes spaces for hosting concerts, festivals, community activities and sporting events.

Sodhi explained that, because of the building’s lit-up impact, approximately ten residential developments have since been built or are under construction nearby, highlighting the role “quality public spaces” can play in wider regeneration.

“Importantly, the value created extends beyond construction economics,” added Sodhi. “Visitors stay longer, businesses benefit from increased footfall, and the location develops an identity that encourages repeat visits and investment.”

According to Sodhi, lighting can also serve as a form of public communication. For example, Philadelphia City Hall’s lighting is programmed to respond to national celebrations, charitable campaigns and civic events, “transforming a historic landmark into a dynamic expression of the city’s identity”.

“Whether celebrating sporting victories or marking important social causes, the building becomes an active participant in public life rather than simply a backdrop,” added Sodhi.

This also applies to Nashville’s illuminated installation, Loqui, Sodhi explained. The artwork includes words and stories from more than 400 local residents and demonstrates how illuminated public art can amplify local voices and bring a community together.

“Rather than lighting serving the artwork, the lighting becomes integral to the experience itself,” he added.

“These projects suggest that good lighting is no longer simply about visibility. It is about participation.”

Sodhi added that buildings are also assessed by how efficiently they operate, but also how effectively they create meaningful experiences.

“Architectural lighting is uniquely positioned to support that ambition,” he explained. “It can extend the usability of spaces after dark, strengthen local identity, encourage social interaction and help transform ordinary infrastructure into memorable landmarks.”

“When thoughtfully integrated from the earliest stages of design, lighting becomes a strategic investment rather than an aesthetic upgrade,” he added. “Perhaps this is the real measure of good design.”

#9152. how ecoLogicStudio uses living organisms to build better spaces for living

architecture need not exclude microbes: these projects use algae, fungi and bacteria as active parts of healthier living environments.

In 2025, a forest emerged in the Triennale Design Museum in Milan. It was DeepForest³, a project by the London-based design studio ecoLogicStudio, co-founded by Claudia Pasquero and Marco Poletto. It was presented as part of the exhibition We the Bacteria: Notes Toward Biotic Architecture, curated by Beatriz Colomina and Mark Wigley, who authored the book of the same title. While the installation looked as though a few saplings had risen from the shiny museum floors, what was on display was, in fact, a hypothesis about how domestic space could be transformed by processes inherent to nature, with Poletto describing it as a system constructed with a ‘fully functional and tangible biotechnological living system, grounded in the metabolic cycles of algae and fungi.’

Seeing the deep green cyanobacteria and the lichen growing from a cork bench felt like following a fungi-covered path back through the London-based studio’s projects. Since its inception in 2005 , the duo has proposed a built world that leverages the powers of nature – algae air-purifying mechanisms, waste-digesting mushrooms, and insulation that grows itself – to develop a style of architecture that grows with the environment instead of against it.

Nearly ten years earlier, at EXPO Milano 2015 Future Food District, a pavilion of triangular panels glowing with a flow of green algae was erected in the event’s central square. Called The Urban Algae Folly, the canopy provided shade through the growth of Spirulina, a type of microalgae that is highly nutritious for people while also being an effective CO₂-capturing organism. Here, ecoLogicStudio created a symbiosis between the sun, the algae, and humans. On sunny days, more algae grows in the membrane of the canopy. When a person stands under it to take advantage of its shade, the CO₂ they release continues to feed the system. The project is born from the idea that architecture should work with microbial life rather than attempt to exclude it. Here, algae become active collaborators in shaping the environment, turning a pavilion into a living, carbon-consuming system.

at EXPO Milano 2015 Future Food District, the pavilion of triangular panels was erected in the event’s central square | image courtesy of ecoLogicStudiowhen a person stands under it to take advantage of its shade, the CO₂ they release continues to feed the system | image courtesy of ecoLogicStudio

In Nyon, Switzerland, the studio developed what they call ‘the world’s first biotechnological healthcare garden that combines air-purifying algae cultures with medicinal plants.’ Here, an outdoor space, a kind of circular, tent-like structure made of semi-transparent fabric, provides a respite for its inhabitants. Inside, the circumference is lined with ‘36 large bioreactors in borosilicate glass which contain 350 litres of living green Chlorella algae cultures that can filter a flow of polluted air of 150 litres/minute.’ The project challenges the assumption that healthy spaces must be sterile. Instead, it positions living organisms as essential infrastructure, using algae and plants to create an environment where ecological and human health are interconnected.

an outdoor, circular, tent-like structure made of semi-transparent fabric, provides a respite for its inhabitants | image © Pepe Fotografiabioreactors in borosilicate glass purifies the air with algae cultures | image © Pepe Fotografia

In collaboration with the Synthetic Landscape Lab at the University of Innsbruck, the studio also produced CryoflorE: a model for cyber gardening the city, which expanded this thinking beyond a singular structure and into the urban realm. As part of the MUDAC’s 2025 Solar Biennial, Soleil·s, the project takes the form of a near-hexagonal model resembling a miniature cityscape of high-rises filled with cyanobacteria.

Here, they ‘capture and channel electrons generated through photosynthesis into electrical currents flowing along the copper wires embedded in the streetscape.’ Using the energy-producing and CO₂-capturing potential of cyanobacteria, the studio takes initial steps towards developing a simulation of a city powered by bio-solar energy networks.

In creating DeepForest³, Pasquero remarked, ‘We are now more and more aware that our own nature is cyborgian and collective, and that our own identities extend far beyond the limits of our bodies. We are microbial ecosystems, we are algorithmic networks. It is a necessary consequence that our home becomes an extension of these ecosystems and networks. Our home is our microbiome.’

The installation itself, on the sun-filled upper floor of the Milan design museum, looks like an abstraction of a forest. There are no leaves, dirt, or moss. Instead, there is a careful arrangement of what look like birch trunks, stripped of their twigs and standing upright on a textured floor. These are what ecoLogicStudio calls ‘biodegraders, built from 3D-printed bark-like shells made of algae biopolymers, [which] host living mycelium networks.’ They get their nutrition from coffee grounds and develop a layer of sinewy material that acts as a kind of insulation.

Between these structures are a series of glass containers holding ‘photosynthesizers, 50 liters of living cyanobacteria, actively capture CO₂ from the gallery environment,’ which serve as living, breathing filters. Lastly, there are ‘carbon storers,’ which digest waste material and give life to living lichen. Among these elements are the tubes, seams, and cords that make this environment possible. In this installation, ecoLogicStudio proposes not a traditional space for living, but a space that lives, grows, digests, and filters. It draws on the logic of the forest to propose an alternative way of living, in which human technologies take a back seat to organic processes.

DeepForest³ serves as a case study for the ideas presented in We the Bacteria. Written by Colomina and Wigley and published by Lars Müller Publishers, the book acts as a sequel to their previous book, Are We Human? In We the Bacteria, the authors examine the sterility of contemporary architecture – its impulse to kill bacteria and what we interpret as germs and grime – and reposition this hostility as a threat to both human and planetary health. Within the text, they write, ‘this book is covered in microbes,’ offering preliminary evidence of how pervasive single-celled organisms are. The authors use evidence of disease in industrialized, developed spaces to encourage a return to the microbial, advocating forms of design that embrace environments in which bacteria can thrive.

DeepForest³ serves as a case study for the ideas presented in We the Bacteria | image © Synthetic Landscape Labcover of We the Bacteria by Beatriz Colomina and Mark Wigley | image courtesy of Lars Müller Publishers

Although We the Bacteria centers on the microbial world, it offers an equally useful framework for understanding ecoLogicStudio’s wider practice. Across these projects, algae, fungi, and carbon become active agents in architecture, challenging the separation between the built environment and the living world.

Together, these projects suggest that architecture can do more than accommodate human needs; it can actively support the organisms and ecological processes with which we share the planet. When done intentionally and carefully, these decisions can result in net-positive outcomes for human life as well. In these spaces, bacteria, fungi, and other organisms are not contaminants to be eliminated or resources to be exploited, but participants in the environments we inhabit. The home and the building become parts of a wider living system, proposing a form of mutualism in which human well-being is inseparable from the health of the more-than-human world. Rather than building against the environment, ecoLogicStudio proposes an architecture that works with it, using the capacities of living organisms to rethink how we construct our homes, buildings, and cities.

opening pages of We the Bacteria  | image courtesy of Lars Müller Publishersinternal spread of of We the Bacteria | image courtesy of Lars Müller Publishersinternal spread of of We the Bacteria | image courtesy of Lars Müller Publishers

projects: DeepForest³ (2025), The AirBubble in Nyon (2024), The Urban Algae Folly (2015), CryoflorE (2025)

#9151. Czech Archaeologists Re-Excavate Long-Lost Tombs of Ancient Egyptian High Officials

Czech archaeologists working at Saqqara have re-excavated a group of tombs belonging to high priests and senior officials of Egypt’s Old Kingdom (c. 2686–2181 BCE). The news was first reported by Ahram Online following an announcement by the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities.

Located 20 miles south of Cairo, the Saqqara archaeological site was the main necropolis for the ancient Egyptian city of Memphis, which was founded around 3100 BCE and abandoned in the 7th century CE. The excavations were made as part of a project by the Czech Institute of Egyptology to locate, excavate, and document tombs partially explored in the 19th century and buried again over time. Related Articles Monumental Statues of Ramses II Discovered in Egypt Ancient Fayum Mummy Portrait Gets Fresh Restoration, With Rare Plans to Leave Egypt for Italy

These tombs were first discovered by the French Egyptologist Auguste Mariette, founder of the Egyptian Antiquities Service, between 1858 and 1860. During those years, Mariette identified approximately 160 tombs in the area dating to the Old Kingdom. However, his excavations focused largely on major artifacts while leaving other parts of the tombs unexplored and inadequately documented.

Among the chief monuments investigated by the Czech mission are the tombs of a man called Sabu and his son Ptahshepses, both of whom were high-ranking officials associated with the cult of Ptah at Memphis. The team also excavated and documented previously unknown parts of the tombs, including an offering chapel belonging to Sabu’s wife, Ikhetnefert, which was never found by Mariette.

Located north of the tomb of his son, Sabu’s tomb has exterior walls mimicking the facades of royal palaces, reflecting his high standing. Inside, researchers found well-preserved reliefs depicting Sabu and Ptahshepses overseeing processions of offering bearers.

Ikhetnefert’s chapel contains a false door decorated with scenes of Ikhetnefert with her husband and their two sons, Peahshepses and Raneferef. According to Miroslav Bárta, head of the Czech team, it is one of team’s most important discoveries, providing new insight into the family and its relationships.

The mission also succeeded in locating the tomb of Ptahshepses through a combination of satellite imagery and field surveys. Here, the archaeologists found the untouched remains of his mummy inside a limestone sarcophagus. Their subsequent analysis indicated that he was over 60 when he died, making him exceptionally long-lived for his time.

According to surviving written sources, Ptahshepses held senior positions under four Fifth Dynasty kings: Sahure, Neferirkare, Raneferef, and Nyuserre. He was the first non-royal to marry an Egyptian princess, Khamaat, daughter of King Userkaf, the founder of the Fifth Dynasty.

In a statement, Hisham El-Leithy, Secretary-General of Egypt’s Supreme Council of Antiquities, explained that the significance of the Czech mission’s renewed investigation lies in its study and documentation of these monuments using modern scientific methods, which are revealing new information about the religious beliefs and social lives of Old Kingdom officials.

As they lift our gaze from our phones, we'll start looking up.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Did you ever see the 2021 Leonardo DiCaprio film Don't Look Up? I don't think it's a spoiler to say that its focus on people not looking up was partly a satire on climate change denial. But more broadly, it fed into the idea that nowadays, we're all looking down a lot; specifically at our phones.

I've honestly got no idea if smart glasses – some of which can now project information, images and videos straight at your eyeballs – will end up taking off in future, and replacing the smartphone. But if they do, then it occurs to me that this will be big news for billboards.

You might assume that if more digital tech catches on, physical advertising would be one of the casualties. After all, why look at a poster when your glasses can show you something tailored? But the more I think about it, the more convinced I am the opposite will happen.

Consider this: nobody is going to wear smart glasses to look at their feet. The whole attraction is that you get the benefits of a phone while keeping your eyes on the world around you. And in most towns and cities – even in this smartphone era – that world is already plastered with outdoor advertising.

And if smart glasses can truly take advantage of augmented reality – tech that overlays digital content onto real-world, physical things – then those billboards will suddenly be a lot more exciting to look at.

For over a century, billboards have been essentially a one-way medium. QR codes promised to fix that, but how many of us have actually stopped in the street, taken out our phones and waggled them at a pixelated square? Once or twice, maybe. But on a regular basis? Hardly.

In future, I reckon, you'll be able to point smart glasses at a billboard and get it to do all sorts of useful things, probably by talking to an AI bot embedded in your specs.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

With a movie billboard, for instance, you might want to play the trailer or find out which cinema it's playing at nearby, and when. You might even want turn-by-turn directions to the multiplex to appear in front of your very eyes.

This might sound like Black Mirror-style sci-fi, but it's worth remembering how many old Black Mirror episodes have essentially come true already. And it certainly seems to be the way the ad industry is thinking.

In fact, you can already see a version of this idea in east London. Electric Garden, on Shoreditch High Street, bills itself as “the billboard you can walk into”. It’s a 21,000 sq ft open-air site that sits behind a row of giant digital screens, so brands can run a campaign on the screens and then build a physical world behind them for people to explore.

Its launch campaign, for Activision’s Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, turned the site into a neon-lit, Seoul-inspired alleyway, complete with convenience stores, plastic stools and code-breaking missions. As co-founder Alex Ezen puts it: “A screen can capture attention, but a physical experience gives people a reason to stop, take part and share it.”

Smart glasses could deliver something similar without anyone needing to build an alleyway. That will make the brief for designers all the harder, of course, but personally, that’s the kind of challenge I’d relish.

Federal student loans offer multiple repayment plans, and choosing the right one can save you tens of thousands of dollars — or cost you the same amount if you choose poorly. The standard 10-year repayment plan is the default and the cheapest option in terms of total interest paid. Every other plan either extends your timeline (increasing total interest) or adjusts payments based on income (providing relief now at a higher long-term cost).

The graduated plan starts low and increases every two years, which sounds appealing for early-career borrowers but costs $3,800 more in interest than the standard plan. The extended plan cuts your monthly payment nearly in half but more than doubles your total interest. Income-driven repayment (IDR) plans offer the lowest payments but can extend repayment to 20-25 years, and the forgiven balance may be taxable income (though this tax treatment is waived through 2025 under current law).

For FI-minded borrowers, the standard 10-year plan or an accelerated payoff is almost always the best choice. Lower monthly payments feel good in the short term but cost you years of investment growth on the other side of payoff.

The most powerful student loan payoff strategy requires no negotiation, no refinancing, and no paperwork — just sending extra money each month. Even small additional payments create dramatic results because they reduce principal directly, which means less interest accrues in every subsequent month.

Here is what extra payments do to a $37,000 loan at 6% interest on the standard 10-year plan.

The math is striking: $100 per month in extra payments saves $4,700 in interest and frees you from student loan debt 3.5 years sooner. That is 3.5 years of $411 monthly payments — roughly $17,300 — that you can redirect to index fund investing instead of sending to your loan servicer.

When making extra payments, explicitly instruct your servicer to apply them to principal, not to advance your due date. Many servicers default to "paid ahead" status, which counts extra payments as future monthly payments rather than principal reduction. Call or submit written instructions that all extra payments must be applied to the principal balance immediately.

The FI angle here is powerful: every month you cut from your student loan repayment is a month your money starts compounding for you instead of against you. A 25-year-old who pays off $37,000 in student loans in 5 years instead of 10 and then invests $411 per month for those freed-up 5 years accumulates roughly $30,000 in additional wealth by age 35.

Beyond extra payments, three strategies can significantly accelerate or reduce your student loan burden: refinancing for a lower interest rate, qualifying for Public Service Loan Forgiveness (PSLF), and leveraging employer student loan repayment benefits.

Refinancing replaces your existing loans with a new private loan at a lower interest rate. If you have strong credit (720+), stable income, and a low debt-to-income ratio, you may qualify for rates 1-3 percentage points below your current federal rate. On a $37,000 balance, dropping from 6% to 4% saves about $4,200 in total interest on a 10-year term.

PSLF forgives the remaining balance on Direct Loans after 120 qualifying payments (10 years) while working full-time for a qualifying employer — government agencies, 501(c)(3) nonprofits, and certain other public service organizations. The forgiven amount is not taxable, making PSLF the most valuable student loan benefit available.

To maximize PSLF, enroll in an income-driven repayment plan to minimize your monthly payments during the 10-year qualifying period. Lower payments mean a larger remaining balance at forgiveness — and since the forgiveness is tax-free, every dollar of reduced payment is a dollar you can invest during those 10 years.

A growing number of employers offer student loan repayment assistance as a benefit — typically $100-$300 per month or $2,000-$5,000 per year toward your balance. Under current tax law, employers can contribute up to $5,250 per year tax-free toward an employee's student loans. Ask your HR department if this benefit exists — it is one of the most underused benefits in corporate America and directly accelerates your path to debt freedom.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

When you send extra money to your student loan servicer, they may apply it as an advance on future payments rather than reducing your principal balance. This means you are technically "paid ahead" by a month or more, but your principal — and the interest accruing on it — remains the same. Contact your servicer (by phone and in writing) and explicitly request that all extra payments be applied to the principal balance immediately. This ensures every extra dollar reduces what you owe and saves you maximum interest.

Student loan payoff is calculated using an amortization formula that accounts for your principal balance, interest rate, and monthly payment amount. Each payment covers accrued interest first, with the remainder reducing principal. Extra payments go entirely to principal, which reduces the interest charged in every subsequent month and accelerates your payoff date.

For most borrowers, yes — especially those with rates above 5-6%. Paying off a $37,000 loan just 3 years early saves $4,700+ in interest and frees up $400+ per month for investing. The exception: borrowers pursuing PSLF should make minimum payments to maximize forgiveness, and those with very low rates (3-4%) may benefit more from investing the extra money.

Refinance if you have strong credit (720+), stable income, and no plans to use income-driven repayment or PSLF. Refinancing to a lower rate saves money, but you permanently lose access to federal protections. Never refinance if you work in public service or may need income-driven payment flexibility.

SAVE (Saving on a Valuable Education) is the newest income-driven repayment plan for federal student loans. It caps payments at 5% of discretionary income for undergraduate loans (10% for graduate), provides an interest subsidy that prevents your balance from growing if payments do not cover interest, and forgives any remaining balance after 20-25 years.

Yes, you can deduct up to $2,500 per year in student loan interest paid, even if you do not itemize deductions. The deduction phases out at higher incomes (MAGI of $80,000-$95,000 for single filers). This deduction effectively reduces your loan's interest rate by your marginal tax rate — a 6% loan costs roughly 4.5% after the deduction if you are in the 22% bracket.

Federal student loans are discharged (forgiven) upon the borrower's death or total and permanent disability, with no tax consequences. Private student loans vary — some have death discharge provisions, others do not and may pursue the estate or a cosigner. If you have private loans with a cosigner, consider term life insurance to protect them.

Your student loan payoff date is not set in stone. Extra payments of just $100 per month can cut years off your repayment timeline and save thousands in interest. Use the right repayment plan for your situation — standard 10-year for aggressive payoff, income-driven if pursuing PSLF, and refinancing if you qualify for a significantly lower rate. Every month you cut from your student loan timeline is a month your money starts building wealth instead of paying interest. Debt freedom is the first milestone on the path to financial independence.

#9148. Tattoo Enthusiasts Have One More Week to Get a Rembrandt Inked for $400 or Less

Fans of both body art and the Dutch Golden Age have one more week to book an appointment for a Rembrandt-themed tattoo at the Rembrandt House Museum.

The museum—located in the artist’s former canal-side home in central Amsterdam—is halfway through a two-week public event called “The Poor Man’s Rembrandt Project,” organized with the renowned 74-year-old Dutch tattoo artist Henk Schiffmacher and his studio. (The Rembrandt House Museum held a similar event with Schiffmacher in 2023.) Related Articles London's National Gallery to Exhibit 40 Works, From Rembrandt to René Magritte Van Gogh Museum Reaches Agreement with Dutch Government on Contentious Renovation Budget

This fall’s event wraps up on November 7, and at press time, slots are still available with Schiffmacher or one of the six other tattoo artists who have opened up a temporary studio in the museum. Clients can book sessions ranging from 100 to 350 euros, or about $110 to $390, and choose from any number of designs culled from Rembrandt’s drawings and etchings.

Options include one of the artist’s recognizable self-portraits; a palette adorned with Amsterdam’s triple-X coat of arms; Hansken, the famous elephant that Rembrandt drew when she toured Amsterdam; and a number of other figure groupings and scenes.

As part of the project, Schiffmacher put out a call for someone willing to have Rembrandt’s The Descent from the Cross tattooed onto his back. About 50 people expressed interest, Schiffmacher told the New York Times, but many had scars or birthmarks that would interfere with the design. Enter production designer Bo Kwakernaak, a “completely clean, young man with a beautiful back,” according to Schiffmacher. He and his colleagues have been collaborating on the post-Crucifixion scene over several sessions.

The museum doesn’t see this public tattooing event as a gimmick. Epco Runia, the Rembrandt House’s head of collections and research, thinks there is a real connection between the prints Rembrandt made (which make up most of the museum’s permanent collection) and the art of tattooing, in that both are effective tools of image dissemination. “I think [Rembrandt] would have some kind of click with Henk Schiffmacher,” Runia told the Times. “They have a little bit the same kind of character.”

#9147. Al-Jawad Pike refreshes Aesop store with terracotta-tiled counter evoking ancient Persia

Photography by Ollie Tomlinson

Local studio Al-Jawad Pike has given skincare brand Aesop’s shop in London department store Harrods a revamp, centred on a terracotta-clad counter designed to have “the qualities of a miniature building”.

Aesop has had a counter in Harrods for over a decade. For this revamp, Al-Jawad Pike, which is a long-term collaborator of Aesop’s, aimed to take the design further than a regular beauty-brand counter.

“We were interested in giving the counter the qualities of a miniature building, with suggestions of apertures, openings and floor levels: something designed with the architectural ambition of a building but the care of a cabinet,” Al-Jawad Pike co-founder Jessam Al-Jawad told Dezeen.

“Through carved alcoves we also wanted to recall the architecture of ancient Persia – the highly literate civilisation that developed liquid perfumery.”

The studio drew on Harrods’ easily recognisable red brick facade when designing the central counter, which is clad in terracotta tiles from Italy that were chosen for their ability to hold scents.

“We chose glazed terracotta early on in the process because of its connection to traditional fragrance production, but also because of its strong association with Harrods’ iconic facade,” Al-Jawad explained.

The counter is decorated with an alchemist-style design piece, described by Aesop as an “olfactory sculpture.”

Glass vessels filled with fragrances hang from a copper stand, with copper cones that let visitors experience the different scents.

“The olfactory sculpture is something that Aesop has been independently developing in different forms across a number of their projects,” Al-Jawad Pike explained.

“Our take on this was to create a delicate but organised structure of copper piping and blown glass, through which fragrance-infused air is pushed to scent funnels for customers to interact with.”

The colour palette of the Aesop store complements the monolithic terracotta counter, with brushed copper brought in as a tactile contrast.

“The colour palette was chosen in collaboration with the team at Aesop for its intensity and richness, which we felt resonated with the olfactory experience of fragrance,” Al-Jawad said.

“We paired this with matte, brushed copper because of its connection to fragrance creation and distillation.”

Earlier this year, Aesop launched its first lighting collection at Milan design week. Previous Aesop stores featured on Dezeen include a Barcelona shop by Mesura that won the 2024 Dezeen Award for best interior.

Photography by Ollie Tomlinson

#9146. carpet diem and 1000 vases merge textile, ceramic, and glass art at espace commines in paris

curator francesco pirrello pairs carpet diem with 1000 vases, using a vertical scenography by hervé sauvage and jean-christophe vaillant to exhibit 32 textile works alongside 100 glass and ceramic objects.

G delaBaume edited by christina vergopoulou November 2, 2026 3 min

Curated by Francesco Pirrello, two international design exhibitions, Carpet Diem and 1000 VASES, converge at Espace Commines in Paris from October 23rd to 25th, 2026. The joint event pairs 32 textile pieces with 100 ceramic and glass objects, creating a unified material dialogue within the historic hall. Through a distinctive vertical scenography, the exhibitions explore contemporary interpretations of craft, form, and material boundaries.

Conceived by Hervé Sauvage and Jean-Christophe Vaillant, the exhibition scenography utilizes a pronounced vertical arrangement to integrate the two disciplines within a singular volume. Rather than isolating objects into segregated typological zones, the layout elevates hanging woven surfaces, embroidered textiles, and sculptural fabrics directly above and adjacent to ceramic and glass vessels displayed on tiered plinths. Carpet Diem showcases diverse fiber manipulations, ranging from structural weaving to experimental surface finishes, while 1000 VASES presents sculptural explorations of the functional vase typology, using glassblowing, slip-casting, and ceramic glazing to bridge functional design and spatial sculpture.

#9145. Will your digital work still exist in 2046? Here’s why the answer might be no

Recently, I’ve written for Creative Bloq's sister site Digital Camera World about a run of photographic rediscoveries. For instance, F Holland Day’s 1898 series The Seven Words resurfaced in September. Then in October, we saw a newly found cache of photos that document the making of the 1926 horror film Faust. These antiquated forms of physical media sat untouched for a century or more, and yet remain totally viewable. Amazing, really.

Now, let's do a thought experiment. If you're old enough, picture the digital work you made 20 years ago. That might be a website design, assets for a CD-ROM, a vector illustration… whatever.

Ask yourself: could you locate and open those files today? If you’re anything like me, the honest answer is “mostly no”.

It's ironic, really. Because digital work has no tangible physical presence, we tend to think of it as eternal. In truth, though, it's kind of the opposite.

This March, I visited memory card manufacturer Lexar’s facilities in Shenzhen, China. And one moment there has stuck with me ever since.

In a press conference, the company's representative explained that the flash memory used in consumer memory cards and SSDs can start losing data within a year if you leave them in a drawer and don't power them up.

Lexar told me it’s developing a dedicated device to address this issue, but it's early days. In contrast, a print just sits there, being a print.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

Meanwhile, if you're putting your work online, there's more bad news. A Pew Research Center study found that 38% of webpages that existed in 2013 were no longer accessible a decade later. Platforms are no safer. Back in 2019, MySpace admitted that a server migration had wiped photos, videos and music uploaded between 2003 and 2015: an estimated 50 million songs from 14 million artists.

Its advice to users was to keep their own backups. But wherever you back stuff up, basically, you're running the same risk. As the sudden closure of Sora highlighted, venture capitalists don't really care about protecting your stuff as much as you do.

There's also the problem of actually opening files in years to come. Built something in Flash in 2012? I doubt you'll be able to salvage it now, after Adobe shuttered the format in 2020, and that's just one example among many.

So what can we do? There are few basic rules we all should be following if we want to be able to access our work in 2030, 2040 and further ahead. The first is to follow the 3-2-1 rule. Keep three copies of anything important, on two different types of storage, with one stored offsite or in the cloud. It's not a foolproof method, but it does reduce the odds of losing stuff exponentially.

Secondly, every few months or so, power up your SSDs and memory cards, so firmware can do its job. Thirdly, export your final files to open formats like TIFF, PNG, SVG or PDF/A, which are more likely to be readable in decades to come.

Fourthly, treat platforms as shop windows, not storerooms. And finally, print your work. As long as you can avoid floods or fires, paper-based storage has a better track record than digital.

Is this seems a bit of a faff, I'd have to agree. But consider this. If future historians end up knowing more about 1926 than 2026, it won’t be for lack of material. It’ll be because we couldn't be bothered to look after it – and what will future generations think of us then?

Tom May is an award-winning journalist specialising in art, design, photography and technology. He is the author of the books The 50 Greatest Designers (Arcturus) and Great TED Talks: Creativity (Pavilion). Tom was previously editor of Professional Photography magazine, associate editor at Creative Bloq, and deputy editor at net magazine.

#9144. Rotterdam's Echo is a Tokyo-inspired listening bar inside the brutalist Groot Handelsgebouw

Photography by Sophia van den Hoek

Creative director Jeﬀ Hoogendijk, DJ and producer Khalil Ryahi and architect Paul Cournet have teamed up to open a listening bar in Rotterdam, featuring a bar made from shipping crates and ombré mirrors by Sabine Marcelis.

Inspired by visits to listening bars in Tokyo, the trio envisioned Echo as a flexible space that can host different events and activities, but primarily focuses on the experience of music.

Located on the ground floor of Groot Handelsgebouw, a post-war office block opposite Rotterdam Centraal station, the bar has an interior designed by Cournet’s architecture and design studio, Cloud.

Cournet said the idea was to adapt the concept of the listening bar to the creative energy of Rotterdam.

“We wanted to make it super local,” he told Dezeen.

The main bar, which functions as both a service counter and the DJ area, exemplifies this approach.

Built in collaboration with Barendregt’s Kistenfabriek, a company that manufactures wooden shipping crates, together with carpenter Simon Fitskie, it’s a reminder that Rotterdam is home to Europe’s largest seaport.

Its sides are printed with the words “handled with care”, which became Echo’s tagline.

“We thought it would be so cool make the bar an art crate because we treated everything, from music to hospitality, as if it were art,” said Cournet.

“We always wanted to do everything in the best way possible.”

The space features several works by Rotterdam-based designer Marcelis, who is Cournet’s partner.

Her signature ombré mirrors adorn the walls, reflecting shades of red and gold, while a linear resin lamp hangs above the bar.

Polish brand Tylko supplied much of the furniture, including the modular shelving that extends across the walls to create space for displaying vinyl.

Cournet previously worked with the furniture company on its Berlin showroom, a project that led to a collaboration with audio company Form Follows Frequency.

Together, they developed a colourful system of speakers and subwoofers that slot precisely into Tylko’s shelving, which launched earlier this year.

These speakers form part of the sound system for Echo, along with two sculptural speaker towers that stand either side of the bar.

“There’s a contrast between the rawness of the exposed concrete and the more refined elements, like the sound system or Sabine’s mirrors,” said Cournet.

“When you put them together, it creates a tension that I find interesting. The concrete feels a bit softer.”

ECHO is one of several listening bars to have opened recently – with others including Bar Bardo in Milan and Upstairs at Hausu in London – but it is the first of its kind in Rotterdam.

The space shifts from a coffee shop by day to a bar by night, and includes a curated retail offering.

It can also morph to accommodate exhibitions, listening sessions of 20 to 40 people, or seated dinners for up to 40 guests.

Since opening in early September, the team has invited various local record stores to contribute to the event programme.

“Rotterdam has this really long history with music, with a lot of famous DJs and people who were pioneers in the music scene in the 1990s and 2000s,” added Cournet.

“It feels like the project has really resonated with that community.”

Photography by Sophia van den Hoek

#9143. Remembering Dolores Huerta: Artists Barbara Carrasco, Judith F. Baca, Yreina D. Cervántez, and Vincent Valdez Reflect on the Iconic Activist’s Legacy

“It’s hard to believe this amazing icon is gone from our world,” artist Judith F. Baca said of Dolores Huerta, the labor activist who died last week at 96.

A cofounder of the United Farm Workers of America, Huerta is best-known for her decades-long dedication to fighting for the labor rights of farmworkers in the fields of California and more broadly for helping to galvanize the Chicano civil rights movement. She recruited members to the union’s cause, led strikes and ensured that companies felt the impact of the absence of the farmworkers whom they exploited, and negotiated the contracts that provided material change to the lives and working conditions for campesinos and campesinas. “She turned the phrase ‘Sí, se puede!’ into a chant that animated rallies and marches well into a new century,” as the Los Angeles Times put it.

“She was always conscious of having women be at the table,” artist Barbara Carrasco told ARTnews, noting that as a UFW negotiator Huerta, one of the few women in a leadership position, was labeled “the dragon lady” for her fierceness. Carrasco said she will always remember Huerta as a nurturing figure who mentored countless women over the decades.

After leaving UFW in the 1980s, she would continue to advocate for labor rights and women rights. In 2002, Huerta received the Puffin Prize for Creative Citizenship, which came with a $100,000 grant. She decided to use the funds start her an eponymous foundation, which aims to “cultivate empowered volunteer organizations actively pursuing social justice,” according to its website.

Huerta’s status as an icon has also translated into the art world, with numerous artists depicting her image over the years, including Baca, Carrasco, Yreina D. Cervántez, and Vincent Valdez, all of whom share their memories of Huerta below.

b. 1955, El Paso, Texas; lives and works in Los Angeles

I first met Dolores when I was around 19. My boyfriend at the time was UCLA student, and I heard Cesar Chavez speak on campus, and I was really impressed. I met Dolores right after, and never in my life, I have met a more charismatic lady. She was just so down to earth. That’s what always struck me about her: Here is this woman with all these accolades are given to her, but she still is such a great human being. She’d meet people—it didn’t matter if they were rich or poor—and she’d treat them all the same. I think that’s what struck a lot of us; we would just say, “Oh, this lady’s amazing.” I went to an UFW convention once, and so many farmworkers came up to her, and they just loved her. That doesn’t happen overnight. That takes years and years of dedication and of being out there and representing them. There’s a quote by her: “Every moment is an organizing opportunity, every person a potential activist, every minute a chance to change the world.” I think she really did take advantage of her time here on Earth.

I’m one of many, many women whom she nurtured and helped. There are so many women, from women in public office to women working in the fields. She always had such pride in the women she mentored. She was also very supportive of visual artists. I remember the night before an event for the Department of Labor, when Hilda Solis was secretary, Dolores asked me to write a list of all the artists who had contributed to the UFW over the years. During the event, she mentioned everybody. I thought, Who does that? Not too many people will pay tribute to the artists. The artist are often the last individuals to be thanked [in a political movement].

In the ’90s, Self-Help Graphics did a women’s atelier [series of prints]. I invited 10 women to join, and I remember saying we should do a print showing women as nurturers. I wanted to pay tribute to Dolores—that was who came to mind immediately. When you do something and you really truly believe in it, it shows. I truly loved her, and I wanted to show that. The colors were specifically chosen: the yellow ocher reflects the good energy coming from her, the blue-green background represents the fields and the farmworkers she was defending in those fields, the rose represents her strength and beauty, both inward and outward. I always thought she was so beautiful and a beautiful soul, too. It was a work I didn’t rush. I was so happy when the Girl Scouts of America selected that portrait to be on a merit patch.

Dolores had a good sense of humor. That was one of our big connections. She and I used to laugh about really silly stuff—if I told you, you wouldn’t believe what we were laughing about it. She always said to keep your inner child alive and not to ignore it. I think that’s why she was able to laugh with so many people and get along with everybody. Her energy was always high, even until the end. We partied together like crazy. At my 70th birthday last year, Dolores was dancing—she loved to dance. She said if she didn’t do what she did, she would have been a dancer.

The last time I talked to her on the phone was about two weeks ago. I got a chance to tell her that I loved her. A lot of us who have been friends with her were lucky enough to see her right before she started treatment. It took her faster than everybody thought. I know firsthand what that kind of treatment is like; I’ve been cancer-free now for some 30 years, and I remember how brutal that kind of treatment is, and I was young, and she was 96. It’s got to be really difficult. She told me she was in a lot of pain. Even though we knew the day was coming soon, it was still a sad day for all of us. She was one of those people who was extremely energetic. When everybody would be tired, she would say, “Come on, let’s do this, and let’s do that.” It was inspiring to be around her.

b. 1946, Los Angeles; lives and works in Los Angeles

Early on in the movement, Dolores and I would have been present at similar things, marches and organizing events in support of the United Farm Workers. I was also at La Paz working at one point [around 1974] to produce a big mural that Carlos Almaraz had designed. I remember painting a section that said, “No More Sweetheart Contacts,” and that piece was used for a march to Sacramento. The making of that giant canvas was the first time I went to La Paz. I might have met her then, but I knew her from a distance for a while. I can’t quite remember when I started to have more personal contact with her.

At a certain point, I had a chance to speak with Dolores at length, and she told me that she was not given the credit that she was due as a cofounder of the United Farm Workers and for the work that she had done. Of course, I understood that because I had struggled myself with the dominance of men within the mural movement and the Chicano movement, and in the art world as well. So, when I started working on Arch of Dignity, Equality and Justice (2005–08), which is a 25-foot arch on the campus of San Jose State University, I decided when I was going to put Dolores in the front of the monument—that she would be the dominant figure, not Chavez. I depicted her in a thoughtful way: One of her hands is outstretched, saying, “Join me,” and is welcoming, and the other hand is a fist. In other words, she was both those things simultaneously. It is a depiction of her in leadership role, coming up out of the fields. From that point on, when I was making something historical, I looked to Dolores as a way to represent the power of a Chicana organizer and a model for us in social activism. In a sense, she was a hero for me over and over again.

She had the most amazing energy I ever experienced—never tiring. Not only that, but you could end up dancing all night with her. I remember staying up until three in the morning with her listening to music at Burning Man in the tent. I have a fabulous image of her in a dust storm there. I couldn’t even get out of the car; it was so horrible. I put my head out and I was choking, and there she was standing there laughing. I thought, How did she get that tenacity, that resilience? It must have been from being out in the Central Valley and having dealt with bad conditions like that in the field. So that to me was a real image of her resilience and her capacity to withstand any storm.

In Gente del Maíz (2012) for the Miguel Contreras Learning Center, you see Dolores in the fields [on the left] with a bullhorn. That comes from a story that Maria Elena Durazo [then executive vice president of the national AFL-CIO Executive Council] told me about how Dolores had called Miguel Contreras to join the United Farm Workers. Later, of course, he joined the United Farm Workers and led the Delano Grape Boycott in Canada. I wanted to indicate that here was this young man, Miguel, who didn’t have a plan to become an activist. It was through Dolores’s encouragement that he joined the movement, and he became a critical figure in it. The central image is an ear of corn with three figures: a young Miguel drops soil, another drops kernels in the soil, and the other is watering the soil. Out of these planted corn kernels come community organizers. I was talking about how there’s the planting of people, the nurturing of souls that become engaged in in a passionate commitment to social justice. I think that’s what Dolores models for us repeatedly: a lifelong commitment to social justice. That’s something important for young people to learn, because they often don’t have an understanding of what it takes to commit a life to creating change. I think more young people need to learn activism is something that you put your body on the line. Dolores was arrested around 25 times, and she was beaten almost to death in San Francisco by the police and they ruptured her spleen. Dolores put her body, her heart, and her spirit into the movement.

In Seeing Through Others’ Eyes (2010), she is there between Chavez and Robert F. Kennedy leading the crowd, while these two men break bread. It’s important to say that we can’t let the discussion of Dolores Huerta focus on her being victimized by Cesar Chavez. It cannot be about that because that’s a diminishment of her character. She was much larger and much more powerful than simply a rape victim.

Dolores was a model, not only training young people to become activists but also she’s a model for standing up against the most powerful forces. I don’t think I can think of a person who can replace her or that can equal her contributions. She’s the Chicana icon, and she will be sorely missed. She was one of the greatest leaders we’ve had.

b. 1952, Garden City, Kansas; lives and works in Los Angeles

It has been my honor and privilege to know Dolores Huerta, whose influence on me and so many others have been tremendous. Dolores has been a warrior in the best sense of the word: powerful, resilient, compassionate, harnessing her formidable intelligence to fight for the rights of those most vulnerable. Dolores was a feminista, a great humanitarian, resolute, and committed for the long term in the struggle for justice and a better world.

Dolores Huerta has had an impact on many generations of women and men, but she had a very special significance for young Chicanas and Latinas of my generation. Before now there were virtually no positive images of women like us in film or media. She was such an inspiration as one of the first prominent mujeres of our time that was a public figure and activista. Dolores showed us courage and dedication, and what it meant to fight for our dignity, equal rights, and how to show solidarity with diverse peoples and struggles.

I met Dolores in Santa Cruz in the early ’70s when I was student, but I did not get to know her until the ’80s. One of my first encounters with her was in East LA. I was asked to help out for a UFW function organized by Fred Ross Jr. and Dolores was there. We had an opportunity to talk at length. I am grateful for that experience and other times spent in her presence; she was very generous and approachable. I last spoke with Dolores at the birthday party for artist Barbara Carrasco, her dear friend. Dolores looked radiant, peaceful, as always composed. I cherish the memory of her dancing—joyful, celebrating, mighty.

Dolores was a strong advocate for the arts and artists. I am very grateful for the support she showed me and many other artists, especially the mujeres artistas. My heartfelt dedication to Dolores Huerta came in the form of the mural La Ofrenda. Located in the Echo Park community, it was created as part of my graduate thesis at UCLA (sponsored by SPARC and the City of Los Angeles Cultural Affairs Department). The mural was executed with the assistance of talented mural crew(s) with contributions from Salvadoran poet Rossana Perez, Chicana/o poets Gloria Enedina Alvarez, Victor Carrillo, and graffiti artist Eric “Duke” Montenegro. Originally painted in 1989, it is meant as an offering to my community, a prayer to the ancestors for courage, strength, and sustenance. It is about the value of labor, the farmworkers, immigration, political exile, and very importantly Chicanx solidarity with the people of Central and Latin America and their wars for liberation. La Ofrenda highlights the vital role of women in creating transformative change. I thought it most fitting to honor Dolores as the central figure in the mural, a unifying force across many cultures, struggles, and advocate for many just causes.

Unfortunately, many of the issues La Ofrenda depicted almost 40 years ago, including the victimization and persecution of immigrants in the US and worldwide persists with unimaginable cruelty. Let us follow the example of Dolores and make “good trouble” as she did in her lifetime and continue to fight for the rights of immigrants, farmworkers, women, and all people. It is my hope that La Ofrenda be a reminder and inspiration to those that knew Dolores Huerta and those that will learn of her enduring legacy, and immeasurable contributions to humanity. So much love and gratitude to you Dolores, beloved mujer and hermana. You are siempre presente.

b. 1977, San Antonio, Texas; lives and works in Houston and San Antonio

There was no better way to begin my ACLU project, The New Americans (2026), than with Dolores Huerta. Dolores’s legacy remains a powerful testament and reminder—our current struggles are nothing new. Generations before us have long endured and remained steadfast in their commitment to confront and challenge the distorted social realities within the United States. Although my portrait of Dolores intends to pay respect to the elders, it is strategic in its conceptual pose. Despite her age, Dolores’s resilient spirit still burns bright. Her head holds high. She is caught gazing optimistically toward the right side of the page. As the first image in a series of 25 drawings, she leads us forward, eager to hand off the torch to those willing to come next. Dolores Huerta will forever be that reminder to us all—be the stubborn pulse in a dying heart.

The first time Dolores and I met in 2015 was completely random and somewhat surreal. It was a very late night after party in Berlin, after the Berlin Film Festival. It was already 2 a.m. And I left before she did. We met up again in 2023 at the Rothko Chapel in Houston. We sat on a stage together with Cheech Marin and shared stories and ideas together about the intertwining of art and democracy. By the end of the discussion, Dolores had managed to convince the entire audience to stand on their feet. She had several hundred people and a mostly white audience, shouting in unison from the tops of their lungs, “SI SE PUEDE!!” Cheech and I stared and smirked at each other in complete awe.

I last saw Dolores in 2024. We met at LACMA to view my exhibition, “El Chavez Ravine.” We spent a memorable afternoon together. I snuck Dolores a razor blade out of my pocket and asked her to etch her name into the back of the lowrider ice cream truck that was the centerpiece of the exhibition. Her spirit of rebellion was always ready, it seemed. At the tail end of the day, I expressed my idea to create a portrait of her in hopes of using it as a catalyst one day, for a bigger idea. I photographed her hands and face before we parted ways.

And finally, just [last Tuesday], I mailed Dolores a personal letter and package containing her portrait along with the completed series of drawings, The New Americans. [On Wednesday] morning, I heard the news. There is something bittersweet about the thought of this envelope never being opened and read by her. Her spirit was a powerful, magnetic force in life and, now, in memory.

From the first ever touchscreen on Mac to the super bright and colourful 'PROLED' XDR display, there are quite a few candidates for the headline feature of Apple's new MacBook Pro. But judging by the reaction in the room during the launch in LA last week, the most popular addition might not be that new at all.

Readers of a certain vintage will remember the illuminated Apple logo. The light-up fruit used to adorn every Apple laptop, and was a (somewhat distracting) mainstay of cafes, trains and DJ performances. In 2015, Apple unceremoniously killed the illuminated logo, replacing it with a mirrored version. But as of last week, it's back – and it seems people are happy about it.

Now, the cynical among you might think the reason for the addition is to make the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display stand out as new in public. There's always something to differentiate a new Apple product from the previous generation, even if it's simply new colours. But from a distance, this new MacBook Pro looks almost identical to non PROLED models. How are we supposed to quietly show it off in a cafe? With the 'new' illuminated logo, of course!

But the less cynical among you might see this as yet another sign that under new CEO John Ternus, Apple is rediscovering its sense of fun. From the brand's wild new TikTok presence to the colourful (and cheap) MacBook Neo, Apple seems to be stepping outside of its space grey prison and embracing a sense of friendliness we haven't seen for years. And it's going down well.

#9140. fala’s porto house pairs striped marble with playful geometric forms and sculptural interiors

an oversized window disguises two floors, while three distinct columns and colorful details challenge the rules of a compact home in portugal.

On a compact plot in Porto, Portugal, fala atelier has completed a house that makes an unusually generous amount of room for geometry. Named House Around a Column, the 120-square-meter residence occupies a site of just 60 square meters, surrounded on all sides by neighboring buildings. Its black-and-white marble facade immediately stands out, with an oversized window and colorful geometric accents offering the first clues to what unfolds inside. Rather than attempting to disguise the constraints of its location, the Portuguese architecture studio turns them into the starting point for a carefully orchestrated series of spatial and visual surprises.

The site itself is anything but straightforward. Its irregular outline presented the architects with the challenge of fitting a functional residence into a distorted footprint. Instead of imposing a conventional rectangular arrangement, fala takes the plot’s longest wall as its principal reference, developing a set of geometric rules that organizes the interior. A continuous circulation route follows this boundary and connects the house’s different levels. Within an otherwise tightly contained volume, the resulting arrangement emphasizes vertical movement, allowing the architecture to make use of height where horizontal space is limited.

The ground floor accommodates the house’s secondary functions, while the main living area occupies the first floor. Here, a single uninterrupted room extends between two large windows, creating a sense of openness within the compact structure. Above it, an angular opening in the ceiling, reminiscent of an Ellsworth Kelly composition, introduces a double-height void. Two staircases, each with a distinct character, continue the circulation towards the rooftop. Together, these elements establish a sequence of spatial connections that gives the residence a more complex interior than its modest footprint might suggest.

Three columns, one circular, one hexagonal, and one square, punctuate this vertical arrangement, introducing different geometries into the same architectural composition. In the main living space, a triangular kitchen, a striped floor, and an isolated column form an unlikely but carefully considered ensemble. Unusual handrails and whimsical pieces of furniture add further layers to the interior, where almost every element seems to have been given its own particular shape. The apparent playfulness, however, follows a precise spatial logic, allowing fala to reconcile its collection of forms within a relatively small area.

Facing the street, the house presents a graphic composition of black-and-white marble stripes, interrupted by a window that appears almost too large for the building. Its proportions are deliberate: two openings belonging to different floors are visually combined into a single figure, concealing the division between the levels. The facade becomes an exercise in manipulating scale and perception, allowing the architects to give the compact residence a distinctive presence within the dense urban setting. The contrast between the marble pattern and the oversized opening makes the exterior as geometrically deliberate as the rooms behind it

Color introduces another layer of architectural mischief. A pink circle, a yellow triangle, and a green square serve as a handle, handrail, and shutter, respectively, transforming familiar functional elements into abstract shapes. At the opposite end of the house, the narrow rear facade follows a similar graphic logic. Two windows sit beneath a striped cornice, while a hovering semicircular handrail gives the elevation the faint appearance of a mischievous face. With its calculated geometries and unexpected details, fala’s House Around a Column demonstrates how a constrained urban plot can accommodate an architecture that is precise without feeling entirely serious.

name: House Around a Column (fala 143) architects: fala atelier | @fala.atelier location: Porto, Portugal

#9139. New Eames Museum in California Funded in Part by Trump Appointee

Executive Editor, ARTnews & Art in America

A new museum devoted to design legends Charles and Ray Eames in the Bay Area of Northern California received more than $25 million in initial funding from Joe Gebbia, an Airbnb cofounder who is currently a Tesla board member and previously worked with Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), according to a report by SFGATE.

“Gebbia is an unexpected benefactor behind the museum in Marin County,” the publication wrote, after citing the $25-million figure from the North Bay Business Journal. “After co-founding Airbnb in San Francisco in 2007, which helped him to eventually earn over $9 billion, Gebbia turned to politics and joined DOGE last year. President Donald Trump later tapped Gebbia to become the chief design officer of the United States and redesign government websites. In response to Gebbia’s political affairs, Airbnb began distancing itself from one of its co-founders.” Related Articles Getty Institute Teams on Conservation Plan for Eames House in L.A. Deep Listening: Animal Collective & Coral Morphologic Dive Deep into Tangerine Reef

The Eames Institute of Infinite Curiosity is slated to take over the former campus of the Birkenstock shoe company, with a building design by the Swiss architecture firm Herzog & de Meuron and landscape design by Field Operations, the firm behind New York’s High Line park.

Gebbia’s support of the nonprofit represents a considerable chunk. The Eames Institute raised over $165 million in contributions from 2021 through 2024, anchored by Gebbia’s $25 million.

Asked about Gebbia’s connection to the planned museum—with his $25 million making up a significant portion of the $165 million raised between 2021 and 2024, Eames Institute president and CEO John Cary told SFGATE that donors have no outside influence. “Joe’s views are his own and do not reflect the Eames Institute,” he said.
