#9138. Cosmic Leonora Carrington Painting Reemerges at Auction After 70 Years

In a dreamy development for the fall auction season, another Surrealist standout has resurfaced on the market. After seven decades out of public view, Leonora Carrington’s Fil d’Or (1953) will appear at Heritage Auctions in New York on November 10, with an estimate of $250,000–$350,000.

Its title translates from the French to “gold thread,” a term traditionally referring to the delicate metal wire used to ornament luxury textiles. The cosmic bird Carrington depicts appears to be composed of intersecting threads, all emanating from a single source: the golden galaxy pulsing in place of a heart. Related Articles Lehmann Maupin and Gallery Wendi Norris to Collaborate on Two-Part Exhibition Pairing Leonora Carrington and Cecilia Vicuña Almine Rech Announces Collaboration with the Consejo Leonora Carrington and rossogranada

She employed a technique developed by her former partner, the artist Max Ernst, known as grattage, in which layers of fresh paint are scraped with a blade or spatula. The process exposes unexpected shapes and patterns through texture, creating an impression of spontaneous motion, as though the picture were realizing itself.

“By choosing this title, Leonora Carrington shifts focus away from the obvious. Instead, she redirects the viewer’s awareness to consider coexisting, alternative meanings—in this case, her meaning—by experimenting with how we emotionally respond to different thoughts,” Heritage Auctions wrote in its citation. “Ultimately, Fil d’Or demonstrates that words hold multiple meanings, explores how others perceive them, and questions whether they are truly understood at all.”

Carrington created Fil d’Or in Mexico, to which she fled after the outbreak of World War II in Europe. There, she formed a swift friendship with fellow refugees, including the Surrealist painter Remedios Varos and photographer Kati Horna, over alchemy, the occult, and esoteric symbolism.

Carrington died in Mexico City in 2011, at the age of 94. Although she achieved success in her lifetime as both a visual artist and a writer, female Surrealists have experienced an unprecedented surge in market interest over the past decade, thanks in part to Cecilia Alemani’s 2022 Venice Biennale, titled after Carrington’s book The Milk of Dreams. The market reached a high point in 2024, when Carrington’s 1945 painting Les Distractions de Dagobert sold for $28.5 million at Sotheby’s, setting an auction record for the artist. The sale easily surpassed her previous auction record of $3.2 million, set in 2022.

A year ago, a lot of people couldn't quite believe it when Canva made Affinity free. Suddenly, the three paid-for apps obtained through the acquisition of Serif were rolled into a single piece of creative software covering everything from photo editing to vector art and desktop publishing, simultaneously serving as a free Photoshop alternative, InDesign alt and Illustrator alt.

There had to be a catch, and one of the suspicions was that the new Affinity would be unlikely to get regular upgrades or improvements. One year on, Canva seems to be defying those predictions. It added new raw photo editing capabilities last month, with more colour, sharpening and detail adjustments. Today, it's completed things by adding one major element that was still missing for many creatives' workflows: a dedicated Affinity for iPad.

The individual Affinity apps (Affinity Photo 2, Designer 2, Publisher 2) were previously available for iPad before last year's launch of the unified free Affinity for desktop. Users who had bought them could continue using the apps, but they didn't support the new .af file format.

The new single-app Affinity for iPad brings the bulk of the combined desktop software to Apple tablets but designed specifically for a touch-first interface. It also takes advantage of Apple Pencil capabilities like pressure and tilt for sketching or for masking images, as well as Apple Pencil Pro's barrel roll, squeeze and hover features.

The app features Sketch Studio for freehand drawing and sketch-to-vector workflows, and several iPad-first features like a Mask Tool and Sketch to Shapes.

Like on the desktop app, Affinity for iPad uses the same .af file format across sketch, vector, photo and layout processes to make cross-media workflows easier. Non-destructive edits render in real time and there's no need for assets to be exported, converted or remade.

For sketching, there's a brush library with controls to shape each brush, while sketches stay live in the file to build on, rather than trace again. The iPad app also includes Affinity's raw image editing capabilities and the ability to create print-ready multi-page documents.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

AI tools, including Generative Expand, upscaling, denoising, and Decompose Layer to split a flat image into editable layers, are available with a subscription via Canva AI Studio.

An increasing range of major software is now available in the form of dedicated iPad apps, from Adobe's main apps like Photoshop, Illustrator and Premiere to DaVinci Resolve for video editing and Maxon's ZBrush for 3D sculpting. This means the powerful iPad Pro can now be used to its full potential for creative work, allowing more mobile workflows, either for working remotely or simply allowing creatives to take time away from the desk to work in another place before coming back to pick things up on desktop.

Affinity for iPad is is free for individual users and available to download from the iPad App Store now. If you don't already have one, you'll need to create a free Canva account to use the app. A premium Canva subscription is required for AI tools.

#9136. Apple takes "monumental step forward" with first touchscreen MacBook

Apple has revealed its latest MacBook Pro model, which features the technology brand’s first laptop touchscreen and what it claims is “the world’s best laptop display”.

Sixteen years after Steve Jobs described touchscreen laptops as “ergonomically terrible”, Apple has ventured into the market with its new MacBook Pro, which is available from 6 November at prices ranging from £2,899 to £14,549.

As well as being touchscreen, the laptop features a PROLED XDR display, which Apple said is “the world’s best laptop display”, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, 128 gigabytes of memory, 16 terabytes of storage, up to 24 hours of battery life and a thinner, lighter design compared to previous models.

It comes in 14- and 16-inch models, weighing three and four pounds respectively. The laptop was designed to be both portable and a powerful tool for professional creatives on the go, whether they’re working on 3D models or playing musical instruments onscreen.

“The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display is a monumental step forward for the Mac,” said Apple chief hardware officer Johny Srouji.

“PROLED XDR is the world’s best laptop display,” he continued. “And with the magic of Touch coming to MacBook Pro, combined with the game-changing performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max, we’ve created a whole new way for pros to interact with their content, taking their workflows to a completely new level.”

“The new MacBook Pro is the result of the deep integration between Apple silicon, hardware, and software, and there’s simply nothing else like it.”

Aiming to provide an intuitive experience, the Touch technology allows users to scroll through a webpage by swiping, zoom in on a photo by pinching, drag and drop slides in presentations and double-tap a window to fill the screen.

The touch sensor is built into the display panel rather than layered over it, to give the feel of touching the displayed content itself.

To support the Touch feature, Apple redesigned the laptop hinge for better stability and created real-time video stabilisation to smooth the camera feed when using the touchscreen on a video call.

Apple said that the macOS operating system automatically translates touches into clicks, meaning multiple existing apps will work with Touch right away. These include Adobe Lightroom, Blender, Maxon Cinema 4D, Maxon ZBrush, Notion, Canva, Zoom, Microsoft Word, Excel and PowerPoint.

“Graphic designers can now use the entire display as their canvas, no longer constrained by the area of the trackpad when drawing,” said Apple.

“Musicians can play software instruments right onscreen, and app developers can test how Touch performs in their iOS and iPadOS apps directly on the MacBook Pro display.”

Apple said the new PROLED XDR display offers “true-to-life colour and unparalleled brightness and contrast”, made possible by combining OLED technology with algorithms that control light across the display.

“The PROLED XDR display offers tandem OLED technology unlike any other, with deep innovations in its layers that keep brightness and grayscale uniform across the entire display, while minimising internal reflections common in traditional OLED designs,” said Apple.

“It’s all backed by advanced algorithms in the display engine that precisely control each pixel in real time, plus a meticulous manufacturing process and precise calibration of every panel for consistency from display to display.”

The MacBook Pro also has a six-speaker sound system, designed for deeper bass and improved sound clarity compared to previous models, and the Dynamic Island search and notification feature currently used in iPhones.

Other recent releases from Apple include its first folding smartphone, the HomeView dashboard for home controls and the budget-friendly MacBook Neo.

#9135. aditya mandlik explores how water, worms and bees can reshape architecture

the mumbai-based architect explores how ecological gradients and non-human intelligence can transform design, shifting architecture from controlling nature to collaborating with it.

“Post-human utopias” is a productive framework for asking what comes next for the built environment. Architecture and design have largely been organized around a singular human figure, what Rosi Braidotti (2013) critiques as the humanist “Man” who is taken as the measure of all things. The result is a progressively sanitized world where microbes, insects, weeds and damp are shut out in the name of hygiene, control and legibility.

To design beyond this center takes more than a new aesthetic. It asks for a pedagogical and philosophical reorientation of the discipline itself.

At the Studio, we approach the built environment by cultivating multispecies encounters and learning from intelligences, both natural and artificial. Our role is slowly shifting from authoring to curating. If we are to design a postanthropocentric future, we need synthetic frameworks that deliberately bring back the encounters sanitised environments have foreclosed, and that allow collaboration across difference without presuming shared goals.

The framework we use is the gradient: the stepped values between two absolutes within a given domain of behaviour. I end up thinking of it as a computer language of “ones” and “zeros”. In landscape design, for instance, the differential fertility of soil can be read as a gradient of values between 0 and 1, defined relative to the region of intervention. By increasing or decreasing the density of these values, we raise or lower the resolution of the gradient, and that is what allows us to curate it.

When one gradient overlaps another, soil type with moisture or light for example, relationships begin to form at the intersections. These produce differentiated conditions that favour different species, microbial communities and other non-human actors.

This echoes Jakob von Uexküll’s notion of the Umwelt, where each organism perceives and acts within its own world, at its own scale. Such intelligences behave with more nuance than any designer could script. If we read these behaviours as micro-, inter- and intra-transactions, they can be incentivised or disincentivised, and the degree of sanitisation becomes a design parameter to be tuned rather than a binary condition to be enforced.

I explored this curatorial approach in Factory 5.0, a project investigating the material agency of non-human organisms. The pavilion was inhabited by thousands of kingworms within transparent acrylic enclosures, staging an encounter between a synthetic material and a biological agent. I wanted to understand what happens when another organism is allowed to take part in architecture’s transformation, beyond the idea of a finished object.

The kingworms gnawed, perforated and consumed the polystyrene, altering its surface, mass and integrity at a pace, and with outcomes, that I could anticipate and curate but never entirely control. Ingestion, along with microbial activity in the worms’ gut, also contributes to the degradation of polystyrene. I designed the pavilion to accommodate this ongoing process, which moved making away from fabrication and assembly towards a continuum that includes consumption, erosion and decomposition.

The worms were not merely occupants. Their actions became part of the pavilion’s spatial experience.

Moisture is one of the most critical resources, and the most important medium for incentivising these transactions at both planetary and molecular scales. Water connects bodies across species and scales, which makes wetness a candidate for the primary gradient of inter-ecological interaction. It operates from the cell membrane to the watershed.

Almost like a fractalised logic, it connects planetary urbanism, utopian futures and molecular survival along a thin line. A post-human curatorial practice would begin by understanding survival transactions across species, and wetness is central to that understanding.

We are currently working on a modest residence in Lonavala, a hill station in the Western Ghats of Maharashtra, along the mountain corridor between Mumbai and Pune. Steep hills, seasonal streams and exceptionally heavy southwest-monsoon rainfall make the region ecologically rich. Yet the same landscape is increasingly a site of rapid construction, driven by demand for second homes and speculative land trading.

As the built footprint expands, the relationship between architecture and the ecological systems that sustain the region becomes critical. For us, the question was not simply how to insert a house into this landscape. It was how the house could stay in conversation with the water, plants and pollinators that make the landscape what it is.

We began by considering how to re-integrate bees into the local ecosystem, not by introducing another species in isolation but by creating conditions that could support their presence. Bees depend on a distributed ecology of flowering plants, nesting opportunities, water and the seasonal rhythms that connect them.

This led us to treat wetness as a primary design parameter. Rather than draining rainfall quickly off the site, we are examining how its movement, accumulation and dispersion can be curated across the landscape. Gradients of moisture are informing the placement and selection of vegetation, creating differentiated conditions for plants with particular flowering cycles and, in turn, more sustained foraging opportunities for bees. The aim is to re-establish conditions for ecological transactions that become harder to sustain as habitats fragment.

Bees connect the reproductive cycles of flowering plants to the wider ecology that depends on them. Their activity allows vegetation to regenerate, and the flowering plants in turn sustain the pollinators. These relationships are neither linear nor isolated. They form a network of dependencies between plants, insects, soil, water and other organisms.

Wetness thus becomes a curatorial instrument. By understanding how rainfall moves and is retained across the site, we can organise vegetation by moisture requirement and flowering strategy, supporting native bees and other pollinators across seasons. The intention is not to place bees in an unsuitable environment, but to make the site hospitable to the relationships that allow them to thrive.

In this sense, the house becomes a small experiment in extending architectural agency beyond human occupation, using the design of water, vegetation and space to create opportunities for other species to take part in shaping the landscape. As the naturalist Loren Eiseley wrote, ‘if there is magic on this planet, it is contained in water. ‘ Perhaps the post-human utopia begins there.

landscape plan maps planting zones and flowering cycles to support pollinatorsdocumentation from Factory 5.0 shows kingworms interacting with polystyrene samples

Aditya Mandlik is a Mumbai-based architect whose practice explores the intersections of architecture, art, urbanism, and ecology. He holds a master’s degree from the Institute for Advanced Architecture of Catalonia (IAAC) in Barcelona and has collaborated with Moon Hoon Architecture in Seoul and Mias Arquitectes in Barcelona. Alongside his practice at Studio Aditya Mandlik (SAM), he teaches at NMIMS Balwant Sheth School of Architecture in Mumbai and Umeå University in Sweden, serves as a research associate at TU Wien, and contributes to Rachana Sansad’s Academy of Architecture in Mumbai.

#9134. Pace CEO Marc Glimcher Responds to Reports of Financial Losses, Says Gallery Will Open New Location in Europe

Pace Gallery’s CEO Marc Glimcher is looking ahead and washing over the headlines over the last week regarding the gallery’s financial accounts.

“We’re all off the bottom, we just had a record art fair at Art Basel Paris, and we’ve had sellout shows of primarily young artists—everything is turning,” he told ARTnews in a phone interview on Monday, noting that the business is already back in the black and will open a new location in Europe “fairly soon.”

Pace Gallery has been shifting its real estate portfolio recently. Back in June, Pace’s London property was put on the market, with the gallery saying it was seeking a “less corporate” space in the British capital, while in September, Pace announced it was seeking tenants for part of its Chelsea headquarters. Glimcher reiterated that London remains a “great market.” He added, “London is working very well. We are never going to close in London.” Related Articles Pace Reports $5.6 M. Loss for International Business, With Glimchers Pledging to Keep It Afloat Pace Gallery Reports Losses of 35.5 Percent for 2024 With 'Real Change' Underway

He said that many galleries use the city as an international hub where “a lot of work gets done managing Asian and European units. It’s a great place to have headquarters and it carries a lot of weight the way New York does.”

Glimcher hinted that he already has “a couple of amazing choices” for Pace’s next London property, The gallery is currently situated on Hanover Square, taking up 8,600 square feet. The gallery will be “about the same size, and we’re going to a more prime location that fits the model we’ve been working on,” said Glimcher, contending that the business has “done a lot of internal reengineering of the way the companies work together” and that the success of its arms in Berlin and Japan have been “very instructive” to the overall strategy of the business.

Pace Gallery published its 2024 accounts last week with Companies House, the British government’s business register. The filing was 10 months late and recorded a turnover of $67.7 million in 2024, a 35.5 percent drop from 2023, which cashed in $105 million. A pre-tax loss of $2,429 was recorded for 2024 compared to a $6.8 million profit for 2023. (The mega-gallery’s UK registered company, The Pace Gallery Limited, serves as the umbrella company for its operations in Europe and Asia, excluding Tokyo as well as the US.)

Shortly after that, Pace Gallery’s 2025 accounts were published, with turnover dipping 2.6 percent to $65.9 million. “We did a balance sheet shift, which appears to be a loss because we’re changing around the way we invest money and take money from other units and let the money flow through each unit independently,” said Glimcher. “We’re in a process of keeping those units a little more autonomous and self-sufficient, to do that, you have to shift the balance sheet.”

In June, the gallery laid off 50 staffers and dropped 50 artists from its roster, including Keith Coventry, TeamLab, John Gerrard, and Glenn Kaino. (Pace now represents a total of 85 artists.) But now that the dust has settled, Glimcher said the gallery is ready for new life.

“We’re always adding artists and the artists that left the roster were artists [who] we were really not working with,” he said. “There were areas that we were really not engaged with, it wasn’t benefiting them or us. They were not artists that we had a super active engagement with. It’s just about focusing your efforts to do less better than doing more not as well.”

Glimcher said that all galleries have been making changes of late and—at least, for Pace—new strategies are starting topaying off.

“We have had an extremely profitable year already in Los Angeles. The things we’ve done are already bearing fruit, and they’re bearing fruit because the market has substantially changed,” he said. “What we’re doing in London, when we have the space and announce it, it’s going to make a lot of sense to everybody.”

A will and a trust both transfer your assets when you die, but they work in fundamentally different ways. Understanding this difference is the first step to protecting the wealth you have built on the path to financial independence.

A will is a legal document that tells a probate court how you want your assets distributed after death. It names an executor to carry out your wishes, names guardians for minor children, and specifies who gets what. The key limitation: a will must go through probate, a court-supervised process that is public, often slow, and can be expensive.

A trust is a legal entity that holds assets on behalf of your beneficiaries. When you create a revocable living trust, you transfer ownership of your assets into the trust while you are alive. You remain the trustee (controller) during your lifetime. When you die, a successor trustee distributes assets according to the trust document — no court, no probate, no public record.

The bottom line: a will is simpler and cheaper to create, but every dollar and asset in it passes through probate. A trust costs more upfront but saves your heirs significant time, money, and hassle.

Probate is the court process that validates a will and supervises asset distribution. For anyone building wealth toward financial independence, probate represents a direct tax on the legacy you have worked to create.

Probate costs by state — the numbers are substantial:

These costs include attorney fees, executor fees, court filing fees, and appraisal costs. In states like California, probate fees are set by statute — the attorney and executor each get a percentage of the gross estate value (not the net), meaning they are calculated before debts are subtracted.

Probate also takes time. The average probate case takes 6-18 months. Complex estates or contested wills can take 2-3 years. During this time, your heirs may not have access to the assets they need. For a surviving spouse who depends on those accounts for living expenses, this delay can be financially devastating.

A revocable living trust avoids probate entirely. Your successor trustee distributes assets directly to beneficiaries, typically within days or weeks. The upfront cost of creating a trust ($1,500-$5,000) almost always saves your heirs tens of thousands compared to probate costs on a $500K+ estate.

The right choice depends on your net worth, family situation, and the states where you own property. Here is a practical framework:

Most FI families start with a revocable living trust paired with a pour-over will. The trust holds your major assets (real estate, brokerage accounts, bank accounts). The pour-over will catches anything you forgot to title into the trust and directs it there upon your death. You also need the will to name guardians for minor children — trusts cannot do this.

The FI angle: You have spent years building wealth through disciplined saving and investing. A trust protects that wealth from probate fees, public exposure, and distribution delays. The $1,500-$5,000 you spend on a trust setup is a one-time cost that saves your heirs 3-7% of your entire estate. For a $1 million FI portfolio, that savings could be $30,000-$70,000. It is one of the highest-ROI financial moves you can make.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The most common estate planning mistake is creating a trust but forgetting to re-title assets into it. A pour-over will acts as a safety net — any assets not in the trust at death are "poured over" into it. This ensures your trust controls distribution of everything, even assets acquired after the trust was created. The pour-over will still goes through probate for those specific assets, but it prevents intestacy for anything you missed. Review your trust funding annually — check that bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and real estate deeds are titled in the name of your trust.

Calculate your total net worth including real estate, retirement accounts, brokerage accounts, and insurance. If you are under $500K with property in one state, a will may be sufficient. Above $500K or multi-state property, a trust is likely worthwhile.

For most FI families, a revocable living trust plus a pour-over will is the optimal combination. The trust avoids probate for major assets. The will names guardians for children and catches anything not in the trust.

Simple wills can be created with online services like Trust & Will ($159-$599) or LegalZoom ($199-$399). Trusts are more complex — consider an estate planning attorney ($1,500-$5,000) for a properly funded trust.

Creating a trust document is only half the job. You must re-title assets into the trust: update deeds for real property, change bank and brokerage account titles, and assign trust ownership where needed. An unfunded trust provides zero benefit.

Life changes — marriage, divorce, children, major asset changes, moving states — all require estate plan updates. Set a recurring calendar reminder to review your documents with an attorney.

A will goes through probate court after you die — a public, court-supervised process that takes 6-18 months and costs 3-7% of your estate. A trust avoids probate entirely. Your successor trustee distributes assets privately, typically within days or weeks.

Yes, in most cases. A trust handles your major assets and avoids probate. A pour-over will catches anything not titled in the trust and names guardians for minor children. Together they provide comprehensive coverage.

A revocable living trust typically costs $1,500-$3,000 through an estate planning attorney. Complex trusts or those involving tax planning can cost $3,000-$10,000+. Online services like Trust & Will offer trust packages starting at $399-$599 for simpler situations.

You can use online services for a basic revocable trust, but the risk of errors is significant. An improperly funded trust — or one that does not comply with your state laws — provides no benefit. For estates over $500K, professional help is strongly recommended.

No. A revocable trust offers no creditor protection because you maintain control of the assets during your lifetime. Only irrevocable trusts provide asset protection, because you permanently give up control of the assets placed in them.

Your state's intestacy laws determine who inherits your assets — usually your spouse and children, but not necessarily in the proportions you would choose. Intestacy also goes through probate, and the court appoints an administrator. It is the most expensive and least predictable outcome.

It's been a while since I saw an optical illusion good enough to share, but I couldn't resist this one, which is like a combination of two of our favourite ever optical illusions. I present: the spinning horse meets the blue and black or white and gold dress – and it's baffling the internet.

This is a real life video of a horse standing in a stable. And the horse is clearly black... except, it isn't. Apparently it's white. I absolutely cannot see this however many times I come back to it, but people in the comments have learned how the horse is actually in shadow, clicked off and back onto it, and then can see that it's white.

I'll share it below – can you see the horse as its real colour, or are you stuck in the same camp as me?

With 4,500 upvotes on Reddit, the r/opticalillusions subreddit is taken with this illusion.

"It's the exact same effect as the White/Gold Blue/Black dress," explains another. "It's an image where the subject is in shadow but the background is in bright sunlight and our brain struggles to differentiate the two lighting conditions."

Other comments share tips on how to achieve the effect if you're struggling.

On Wednesday night, ARTnews and Hublot hosted a dinner at the New York headquarters of artist and fashion designer Kid Super (Colm Dillane).

Guests included collector Carla Shen; Frank Suznjevic, president of Hublot Americas; ARTnews and Art in America editor-in-chief Sarah Douglas; Time to Drive festival founder Perri Dash; fashion designer Mobolaji Dawodu; collector Viljon Caka; Gazelli Art House senior director Haley Shaw; filmmaker Saam Farahmand; collector and commentator Jeff Magid; gallerist Adam Cohen; artist Jonathan Gardenhire; Brooklyn Museum trustee Carla Shen; curator Anwarii Musa, and real estate developer Ben Levine. Related Articles Pace CEO Marc Glimcher Responds to Reports of Financial Losses, Says Gallery Will Open New Location in Europe Cosmic Leonora Carrington Painting Reemerges at Auction After 70 Years

PJ Monte of Monte’s Fine Foods, also known as the Sauce Boss, provided dinner.

In a conversation with Douglas, Dillane said he had first found the art world somewhat inaccessible, and he compared his entrée into it to the reception he got early on in fashion. “I was really an outsider [there] as well,” he said. “I got rejected three times from the official calendar [at Paris Fashion Week]…. [T]hey finally said yes. Once I broke into fashion, I realized that behind this wall there’s really interesting people who care about new ideas.”

Dillane gave attendees a tour of his 10,000-square-foot headquarters. The building includes a Hublot-sponsored rooftop soccer pitch, an art studio, a podcast studio, a store, and other spaces for all kinds of creative work. “When everyone got here, I couldn’t wait to tour them around the building,” Dillane told the guests. “This is my greatest work, and I think it encapsulates [my] whole practice.” Of the many creative avenues he has pursued, he said, “For me, all of these different mediums were pushing towards the same spirit…. There’s a mischievousness to it…. There’s bringing people together. I want to capture the feeling that I feel when I’m in New York, where anything feels possible.”

#9130. "Lady in Blue is as fitting a monument to our era as any I can imagine"

Tschabalala Self’s sculpture is far from being out of place in Trafalgar Square, writes Priya Khanchandani.

Who belongs in public space? How should public art represent who we are? And who deserves to be celebrated, cast in bronze and placed on a pedestal? These are some of the questions that Tschabalala Self’s commission for the Fourth Plinth, Lady in Blue, has raised in recent months, since it was unveiled in September.

I was there that cloudy morning in Trafalgar Square – a space I’d always crossed, probably like most Londoners, without thinking much about what it symbolises. When the black cloth was pulled away, we saw the figure of a Black woman caught mid-stride, one leg pushing through the fabric of her bright blue dress.

Like most of the admirals and generals monumentalised around her, she is cast in bronze. But unlike them she isn’t posed in command, she’s on her way somewhere. Her head, hair piled high, looks straight out into the city towards Whitehall, her left arm and fingers outstretched, moving with intention.

My Instagram post about the unveiling alarmingly attracted more than 6,000 comments, many of them either subtly or openly racist

I couldn’t help but feel satisfaction that a sculpture of a Black woman was there, taking up space in the city, on what is probably the most visible public plinth in Britain, and assumed this sentiment would be widely shared. It turns out I was wrong; my Instagram post about the unveiling alarmingly attracted more than 6,000 comments, many of them either subtly or openly racist and often suggesting the sculpture doesn’t fit its context.

I feel the need, therefore, to address the notion of what and who belongs in public space, and particularly in a space like Trafalgar Square.

Before Trafalgar Square existed, the site was used for the royal stables that served Whitehall Palace. Designed in 1840 by Charles Barry, the square was conceived as a stage for Britain’s image of itself, articulated through the grandeur of neoclassicism, and statues were central to its story. If you linger, you’ll spot George IV in Roman robes, sitting valiantly astride his horse. The generals Henry Havelock and Charles James Napier, whose reputations were made in the violent consolidation of British rule in India (the latter for the conquest of Sindh, where all four of my grandparents happen to be from) stand on two further plinths.

Admiral Horatio Nelson himself, the Royal Navy officer whose victory at the Battle of Trafalgar gave the square its name, overlooks them from 50 metres high atop a granite Corinthian column, guarded by four bronze lions. This composition represents a particular vision of 19th-century imperial power, reflected in the monuments and civic spaces rolled out across the Empire.

The square might be beautiful, and a fitting monument to its time, but it is also a living, breathing entity formed not only through its monuments and buildings, but also through the way it has been used.

Its function and meaning as a civic space keep being shaped by the people who have held festivals, memorials, gatherings here – or even simply walked through it on their daily commute. After it was built, Trafalgar Square quickly became a place for public assembly. From Bloody Sunday to the suffragettes to Black Lives Matter and the Palestine Coalition, it has a long tradition as a space of protest.

The square has been redesigned over and over, most significantly by Foster + Partners and Atkins in a 2003 scheme that closed the road along its northern edge, adding a terrace and turning what was essentially a traffic island into a pedestrianised space.

For some, in recent years the commission has merely settled into a pleasant biennial ritual

Lady in Blue is in dialogue with this context. She echoes the other figures here through her medium, bronze. And yet while the other figures are rooted to their respective plinths, she looks frozen in motion, echoing the movement of the people in the square below rather than the stillness of statues. The vivid blue of the figure’s dress – evoking lapis lazuli, the stone that has been ground into pigment since antiquity – is far from an attack on the Western canon, but rather in conscious conversation with it.

Once intended for an equestrian statue of William IV, the Fourth Plinth stood empty for more than 150 years before it became a space for contemporary sculpture in 1998. Unoccupied, it was always suggestive of a history waiting to be told or – given that the sculptures around it were all commemorating a contemporary moment – a future moment waiting to be solidified in bronze.

The absence of a statue suggested the question of who belongs on a pedestal was always open. Its dedication to contemporary art has allowed for redefinition and offered a chance to bring a quite spectacular historic space, a space of democracy, protest and celebration, into sync with the present.

The Fourth Plinth has become a space where identities are made visible and histories challenged, from Marc Quinn’s powerful Alison Lapper Pregnant, to Yinka Shonibare’s sculpture of Nelson’s own ship in a bottle. Works like these have also, at times, provoked arguments about how the square should be used, and yet each of them has become a part of its changing meaning.

For some, in recent years the commission has merely settled into a pleasant biennial ritual – and yet, this year’s sculpture underscores why it exists and why it’s so necessary right now.

In 2026, when a Black woman crossing this space is one of the most ordinary sights imaginable, Self’s statue validates her as worthy of belonging, not just in the city but here, in a culturally and politically charged public space dominated by white men sculpted by other white men.

Any notion that she doesn’t belong isn’t an aesthetic judgement, so much as a claim about who the city is for

That elevating such a woman into the visual language of the monument should provoke rage is telling, especially when all the figure has done is walk. Any notion that she doesn’t belong isn’t an aesthetic judgement, so much as a claim about who the city is for.

Self has said her work is meant to speak to human experience beyond racial identity. She has described the sculpture as depicting “everywoman”, implying that an ordinary person merits acknowledgement.

In other words, she hasn’t put it into the world simply as a statement about race – though its reception shows how readily the presence of a Black woman in this setting becomes about who is allowed to stand for the universal.

It’s as fitting a monument to our era as any I can imagine. At such a fractured time, I can’t help but feel relieved she is there, elbowing her way through the noise, making room for all of us.

Priya Khanchandani is a writer and curator specialising in contemporary design and visual culture. She was formerly head of curatorial at the Design Museum, where she curated the exhibition The Offbeat Sari and an accompanying book. She was also previously editor-in-chief of Icon, while her writing has appeared in the Financial Times, Frieze, The Guardian and The World of Interiors, as well as numerous books.

#9129. discarded leather armchair deconstructs into nine functional domestic objects

what becomes possible when every material is considered a resource? jan-micha gamer turns a bulky waste leather armchair into a floor basket, a candleholder, a lamp, a fruit basket, a pouf, a picture frame, a cabinet, a carpet, and a table.

Studio JM edited by christina vergopoulou November 2, 2026 3 min

Designed by Jan-Micha Gamer, Raw Material: Armchair, or Armchair as Resource, is a circular design study that deconstructs a single discarded leather armchair into nine distinct functional objects forming a domestic ensemble. Salvaged from municipal bulky waste, the multi-component seating typology serves as a material test case, investigating how complex, heterogeneous consumer goods can be comprehensively repurposed to replace virgin resources without downcycling.

The project by designer Jan-Micha Gamer prioritizes material-driven detailing, mechanical separability, and circular cascades. Gamer began by disassembling the chair’s structural core, upholstery layers, and exterior envelope, sorting the timber, metal fasteners, foam, textile webbing, and worn leather hides. Instead of concealing imperfections, the design adapts production processes around the irregular dimensions and patinas of the recovered feedstock. Joinery solutions prioritize dry, reversible connections over permanent adhesives, and finishes are selected to maintain monomaterial purity for future disassembly cycles. The resulting nine objects—ranging from small tables and storage vessels to adapted fruit baskets lined with reclaimed textiles—demonstrate small-scale decentralized fabrication methods capable of processing non-standardized waste streams into functional domestic products.

floor basket — recovered leather is shaped into a floor basket, carrying the material’s creases and traces of use into a new everyday objectcandleholder — the geometric form of the original beechwood feet is carried into a single candleholder, retaining the character of the original componentslamp — layered geometric forms create the lampshade, while a thin fabric covering reveals the texture of the repurposed upholstery batting beneathfruit basket — the distinctive spring geometry and tension of the armchair’s wave springs are translated into a sculptural bowl, joined with screwable stainless-steel connectorspouf — foam layers of different densities converge into a compact, architectural seating piece, with the geometry of the material defining its final formpicture frame — wood offcuts frame a print of the original armchair; many pieces remain in their original state, preserving their individual charactercabinet — made entirely from greyboard, the cabinet reuses surfaces once covered with foam; adhesive residue and staples remain visiblecarpet — irregular leather pieces form a shape reminiscent of an animal hide, embracing the material’s traces of use as an aesthetic qualitytable — a translucent, hard-wearing coating highlights the unusual grain of the armchair’s low-grade frame timber, turning an overlooked material into a defining featureprocess – applying a suitable coating as part of the finishing process, balancing surface quality, durability and the potential for future material recoverydisassembly – carefully separating the chair’s layers and components to minimise damage and preserve the material fractions for further use

name: Raw Material: Armchair / Armchair as Resource designer: Jan-Micha Gamer | @janmichagamer

Concept artist Christian Forsgren explains how Arrowhead takes hardware from Blender blockout to in-engine testing.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

With the Scope of Authority Warbond bringing new sniper rifles, ghillie armour, and mine grenades to Helldivers 2, we asked Arrowhead concept artist Christian Forsgren how that kind of hardware goes from Blender blockout to an in-game weapon. The answer is speed. “I can see how it actually handles in a player’s hands straight away, not weeks later,” he says. For weapons and machinery, that matters: a badly judged few centimetres can be the difference between convincing military hardware and something from a toy shop.

Each asset starts with a brief and a team brainstorm. Forsgren then builds a rough 3D blockout in Blender, refines the functionality, materials and finish, and pushes it into Arrowhead’s Stingray engine to see how it behaves in real time.

That loop helps give Helldivers 2 its battered, believable look. Weapons have to be mechanically plausible, and procedural materials add edge wear, grime and volumetric detail “without ever doing a single second of UVs”. Forsgren has also built a Blender pipeline for the game’s Warbond banners, producing renders at a higher fidelity than the game itself can manage, in the series’ propaganda-poster style.

There’s plenty here for Blender users beyond games, too: the scripts and add-ons Forsgren uses to speed up his work, the custom tools Arrowhead uses to move assets between Blender and the engine, and why the studio lets artists build their own workflows. The takeaway is that the best pipeline helps artists make better decisions, faster, with fewer hand-offs.

For more on Helldivers 2, visit Arrowhead Game Studios.

Christian Forsgren: It starts with a brief, then it’s team brainstorming. After that team brainstorm I take over and focus on ideas we have landed on and take it to a point where we can start to iterate. Say I'm building a weapon: I take the agreed upon brief and build the concept model in Blender, sometimes I do simple sketches depending on the asset to bounce around the team but most of the time it's straight into Blender for easy blockouts to help with scale and animation approximations. When that has reached a reasonable state I take it further and focus on functionality, materials, and how we want the finished asset to look like.

When that is greenlit Blender's job ends once the asset's ready to live in the game. We push it straight into Stingray, the game engine, and we're play-testing it in real time so I can see how it actually handles in a player's hands straight away, not weeks later. That's where Stingray takes over: real lighting, real scale, how it sits next to everything else. Then it's a loop with coders, designers, 3D artists and animators until it actually fits the game, not just looks good on its own.

CF: My own setup runs on scripts I've built and collected over time. Everything from camera related addons that help me manage the compositor, HDRI’s, Lights, focal length and Depth of field. Addons that help me create procedural materials in the shader editor. Pie menus to help me speed up access to all different kinds of Blender nested menus. The asset library is an insanely helpful addition to Blender to help me keep track of textures, materials, assets, animations and have them always available without opening a file explorer. The ecosystem's incredible and most problems I hit, someone's already solved it.

At a studio level, Arrowhead's built custom exporters and importers to bridge Blender and our engine. The problem we were solving was speed and consistency. Without that bridge, every asset needs manual rebuilding or re-checking every time it crosses from Blender into the engine, and that adds up fast across a whole team.

CF: Military realism drives a lot of it. Every weapon, like the arm-mounted cannons on our Exosuits (the mech suits players pilot in Helldivers 2), has to be functionally plausible, with every part sized to actually fit how it works mechanically. That attention to real, physical logic is a big part of why it reads as lived-in rather than designed.

Blender's procedural tools do a lot of heavy lifting too. I can generate complex backgrounds like planets and star systems without hand-painting any of it, and Cycles with some simple HDRIs gets me high-quality results without a huge amount of manual tweaking. That procedural system is always handy when it comes to the nitty-gritty textures as well; I can get there very fast with the procedural texturing tools inside Blender. All the nodes available to me make it a breeze to create edge wear, grungy textures and interesting volumetrics without ever doing a single second of UV’s.

For the war bond banners specifically, I built a proper Blender pipeline to replace what used to just be in-game screenshots with simple text put on top; now it has grown to larger marketing material where the most important part of the image is made in Blender in conjunction with studio tools to get in-game assets into Blender to be rendered at higher fidelity than we could ever achieve in-game to really row home that gritty propaganda feel we always strive for.

CF: Because we can export an asset into Stingray and see it working within a few hours, we iterate fast, and the feedback loop with coders, designers and animators continues until the design fits the game.

All games go through late asset iterations, it may be because what we initially thought was something fitting of the fantasy has changed because other assets in the game brought this particular one into the wrong direction so now the concept has to change.

Since Helldivers is such a vast world we often find other uses for assets that maybe not made the cut so we try to salvage things at later stages or for different themes just so interesting ideas don’t get lost but since we built the workflow to use 3D early and iterate on blockouts early it rarely happens.

CF: Blender is my all-in-one package for modelling, animation, texturing,simulation and rendering, so I don't have to jump between programs, which is why I prefer it to other 3D packages which are more specific in their use cases. Blender is also the most user friendly, working with other packages was always way too daunting as a concept

artist, but there was something in the way Blender did everything I wanted in the same package that made it a go to choice.

CF: Arrowhead gives us creative freedom to choose our own tools and workflows but we have some specific ones everyone uses to bridge the game engine and Blender. A lot of the 3D artists at the studio have very different setups based on how they like to work, which I think is really important. Pushing everyone to use the same exact

setup can have some advantages, but giving team members the tools to customise Blender how they like to is what keeps that individuality.

The studio-specific tools are there to get finished work from Blender into the engine, not to dictate how that work is made. Everyone has their own setup when it comes to the tools they like to work with, be it specific add-ons if you are an environment artist or if you are a hard surface artist or character artist. All these use vastly different workflows, so empowering them to use what they think is best is super important, and it also helps create an environment where different disciplines can empower each other.

CF: Honestly, it's being able to push early concept blockouts straight from Blender into the engine and have it working almost immediately. I didn't expect that to become as central as it has. It's changed how fast we can actually iterate, because I'm not waiting around to see if something works now we can test animations, scale and overall look within the engine in the blink of an eye.

CF: What transfers, I think, is the mindset more than any specific tool. We lean on Blender because it's open source and shows what you can do without breaking the bank, whether you're a studio or working completely solo, it gives you real, tangible results rather than something generated for you. Having modelling, texturing and animation all in one place matters most if you're working alone and don't want to juggle five different programs.

The other thing that transfers is freedom in your own process. Arrowhead gives artists a lot of freedom in which tools and workflows they use, and everyone on the team works a bit differently. On my end, that shows up in small ways. Procedural tools save a lot of time by generating things like backgrounds automatically instead of building them by hand, and I do colour and exposure work right inside the render with the Photographer add-on instead of switching to Photoshop.

CF: The industry is always changing, so it is very hard to be on top of what works and what doesn’t. But with the knowledge and connections I possess today, I could more easily create workflows that would be in line with how I can work more closely with the rest of the teams. How can we bridge the gap between artists, animators and designers? For example, it’s an everlasting process of building pipelines, so who knows what is on the horizon.

It's time for the world of high quality wired earphones (or IEMs) to get excited, as it's the annual 11/11 sales period, and there are some awesome discounts on already well-priced products.

My absolute favourite would be the Juzear Light Shuttle, which I reviewed only last month. It is my 'neutral with bass-boost' release of the year, and it's currently down from $190 to $155 over at AliExpress.

All six of these IEMs are featured either on my list of the best budget IEMs currently on the market, or my pick of the best IEM under $500.

This is the last IEM that I reviewed, and I was really impressed by its warm/neutral sound, with a textured bass response and clear, clean, yet not over the top treble. Plenty to like about this one, especially its new price of $121.

This is the cheapest IEM on the list, and it's a really good buy. Made of all-metal shells, it's more durable than most $40 IEMs out there, and its take on a V-shape sound signature is fun and energetic. A good all-rounder, though things do get a little spicy up in the treble some times.

This 8-driver IEM is the most expensive IEM on the list, but it's also my favourite. It does musical with smooth upper mids like few other IEMs that I've heard, and there's a fairly big bass shelf in there too for fun. This is smooth and exact, and $251 is an absolute bargain down from $389. Read my Aful Performer 8S review for more.

This two dynamic driver and four balanced armature hybrid IEM is a bit of a classic – and for good reason. It's one of the first to popularise the 'neutral with bass boost' sound signature, otherwise known as New Meta. That means its well balanced in the mids, but has the excitement of elevated bass. One of the best IEMs on the list.

I haven't reviewed the 1900 yet, but I was impressed with its bright/clear sound. It reminded me of its more expensive brother the Binary EP321 – but $100 cheaper. At $157 I think this is another super strong option for the HiFiGo sale.

The MiracleOne is the most recent IEM that I've received, and there's lots of like. The comfort is S tier, and that goes a long way when you've got a crowd-pleasing sound to back it up. #9126. Olaver unveils multi-purpose Laneway Studio with "lantern-like" glass-block facade

Photography by Brook James

In the garden of a Melbourne family home, a facade of glass blocks set within recycled white brick and a concrete band beam tops this two-storey studio by Australian architecture practice Olaver.

Olaver designed Laneway Studio to appear as a “beautiful object” reflecting light into the garden in the day and glowing like a lantern at night. The multi-purpose building was designed in response to the growing needs of the family of five, offering a practical alternative to renovating the existing home.

It houses a study-cum-guest-room with an en-suite and terrace on the first floor and an open-plan living area below, fitted with concealed laundry facilities and a bar.

The new studio block was constructed behind the main house and its newly configured garden, designed by landscape architect Penny Starr to include a pool and areas of planted foliage.

Large glass-panelled sliding doors leading into the garden from both the house and studio create a seamless flow between the interior and exterior living spaces.

Another sliding door on the opposing wall of the studio, made from oak with a steel-clad exterior, connects the studio’s living space with the titular laneway behind the property.

“With large sliding doors on opposing walls, the ground floor can open right through, so it works as an extension of the garden and pool terrace to the laneway rather than a closed room”, Olaver director Emlyn Olaver told Dezeen.

“Open, the space feels far bigger than its footprint, and the family can spread across the house, the pool and the studio as one connected space when entertaining”, she continued.

Inside, the ground floor was designed to be minimal and open-plan to ensure its multi-functionality. It features neutral terrazzo flooring throughout. Oak cabinetry conceals storage, laundry facilities and a TV nook and frames a central bar area with a stainless-steel sink and surround.

“We wanted the studio to be calm, with joinery doing the heavy lifting so each space can change roles without feeling cluttered”, Olaver explained.

“Every space had to do more than one job; a laundry, a living room or a bar depending on the day. That flexibility also gives the building a longer life, because the family’s needs will keep changing as the kids grow up, move out and come back.”

On the first floor’s east-facing wall, overlooking the garden, a facade of glass blocks was installed above a concrete band beam to bypass planning restrictions on the use of conventional windows.

The first-floor interiors were also designed to be multi-functional, comprising a combined study and guest bedroom with an en-suite and small roof terrace. Red wraparound tiling in the bathroom is echoed by red panelling in the nook of the foldable bed, itself concealed behind more oak joinery when not in use.

“The new studio’s interiors echo the existing home’s rich but calm textures,” Olaver said. “Natural materials and tactile elements exist in both spaces, but the studio is slightly more playful in its approach.”

The project tasked Olaver with extending the home of a family rapidly outgrowing their existing space.

“In Melbourne, the usual answer is yet another extension that eats into the backyard,” she said. “Laneway Studio goes the other way, keeping the garden at the centre of the site and showing how a well-designed studio can add flexibility and density to an existing lot.”

More studio developments recently featured on Dezeen include a Camber Sands studio made using waste materials and a green-tiled studio in a London garden.

#9125. Anxiety Tattoos: How Ink Therapy Can Help Ease Mental Health Struggles

Tattoos have long been a flex in personal expression and artistry. For some peeps, they’re the go-to for commemorating life wins or solidifying deep-seated beliefs — from quotes that got you through dark times or portraits of your fave pets.

The act of getting inked can also be a profoundly therapeutic experience. The machine’s buzz and the needle’s sharp sting are part of a ritual that may help bring internal battles to the surface. But is there a link between anxiety and the decision to get tatted? Could framing your fears and anxieties in gorgeous designs help you cope? Continue reading to find out.

For many, tattoos are much more than art. Peeps who have anxiety may get tattoos as a way of taking control over their narrative, including their mental health struggles.

Anxiety disorder makes life challenging, and you may feel you’re stuck in a rip tide of continual worry, fear, and dread. Even if you know it’s the anxiety talking, you can still struggle to contain these overwhelming feelings, and it’s exhausting. Anxiety can trick your mind, tell you you’re unworthy, and there’s no way out.

But here’s where tattoos come into play — they create a visual shoutout to your strength and resilience. Imagine marking your skin with reminders of the battles you’ve won and what you’ve overcome.

Getting inked can feel like grabbing the reins back from anxiety and stress. A tattoo is an affirmation. It can turn your invisible battle scars into something tangible and beautiful, giving a sense of ownership over your body and experiences. This is huge when anxiety tries to convince you that you don’t have a say in your own story.

Whether it’s a poignant quote, a symbolic image, or just a badass design, a tattoo packs a punch of personal significance and your enduring strength. You’ve taken a deliberate, proactive step to help you take greater control over your life, and that should be celebrated.

Psychologically, tattoos are visual high-fives to yourself. For the anxious folks, tats are a way to take those messy, abstract feelings and pin them down in something real and tangible.

There’s also some evidence to suggest that the pain involved in tattooing can be cathartic, offering a physical release for emotional pain. This could explain why people who self-harm or live with substance misuse or eating disorders might be drawn to the tattoo chair — it’s a place where psychological pain is acknowledged and artistically transformed.

Research suggests there may be correlations between tattoos and mental health.

One 2013 study involving 65 female participants living with anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating disorder explored the relationship between eating disorders, self-injury, and tattoos. Around 51% of the participants reported a history of self-injury, and 27% had at least one tattoo. Those with tattoos were more likely to have a history of self-harm, so the authors suggested that tats could be a form of self-punishment.

However, in an interesting twist, 27% of those with tattoos showed no history of self-injury. These peeps reported more positive body image, higher self-esteem, and fewer mental health struggles.

The relationship between tats and mental health is complex and still being decoded. Further research would help confirm the link between the two.

Tattoos can swing either way on the mental health seesaw. For some folks, getting tattooed is symbolic of their healing process. It says, “Hey, I’ve been through some stuff, but look how I’ve grown!” These tattoos often become symbols of a deeply personal journey, spotlighting moments of triumph over anxiety and depression.

But here’s the flip side: if someone gets inked on a whim or during a rough patch without much thought, that tattoo could be a permanent reminder of a not-so-great time.

In a 2011 study of 82 peeps getting their first tattoo, researchers measured their feelings about their appearance and body both before they got the tattoo and then again immediately and three weeks after the tattooing. The findings showed that right after getting their tattoos, folks of all genders experienced a decrease in appearance anxiety and dissatisfaction. Three weeks later, they reported increased body appreciation, a stronger sense of having a distinctive appearance, heightened feelings of uniqueness, and improved self-esteem. However, female folks experienced increased anxiety related to how others viewed their physique 3 weeks post-tattoo, while males reported a decrease in this type of anxiety.

These results suggest that getting a tattoo can positively affect mental health, but of course, the impact varies among individuals.

Tattoos can be an artistic strategy to enhance your mental health game, but it’s crucial to take a beat and really think it through before you get inked.

Whether you’re looking to mark a milestone, manage the mayhem of anxiety, or remind yourself that everything will be okay, a carefully considered tattoo can be a meaningful addition to your narrative, helping you manage anxiety and positively shaping your story.

So you just got a tattoo — congrats! Time to focus on aftercare. If you want your tattoo to age gracefully, the next few weeks are extra important to…

There are a number of reasons a new or old tattoo can itch. Infections, allergic reactions, and preexisting skin conditions are just a few possible…

#9124. matteo thun transforms 72 apartments inside milan’s iconic brutalist torre velasca

working within the protected 1958 tower, the studio pairs original architectural details with velvet walls and italian design classics.

Matteo Thun & Partners has unveiled the interiors of 72 residences inside Milan’s Torre Velasca, the postwar skyscraper designed by Italian architecture studio BBPR. The project occupies floors 19 through 26, and introduces suites and apartments for short- and long-term stays. This includes duplex penthouses overlooking the city. Set to open in phases beginning in fall 2026, the renovated interiors bring rich colors and Italian design classics into one of Milan’s most iconic buildings.

Completed in 1958, Torre Velasca was designed by BBPR on a site heavily damaged during World War II. Its unusual silhouette, with a broad residential volume projecting above a narrower office tower, takes inspiration from medieval Lombard architecture, especially the Filarete Tower at Milan’s Castello Sforzesco. Angled reinforced-concrete supports carry the upper floors, giving the building its distinctive mushroom-like profile. Even after the design stirred considerable debate among modernist architects at the time, it’s since become an unmistakable part of Milan’s skyline.

The new interiors follow an extensive restoration of Torre Velasca led by Milan-based studio Asti Architetti for developer Hines, completed in 2025. For the team at Matteo Thun & Partners, working within the protected building meant accommodating much of its original architecture. Tiles in the kitchens and bathrooms have been preserved, along with historic doors and window frames. The apartments also retain their original loggias, which punctuate the tower’s upper volume and frame vast views across Milan.

The existing proportions presented their own challenges. Ceilings are relatively low, and many of the rooms are compact, prompting the studio to introduce glossy finishes that reflect daylight and give the interiors a greater sense of space. Floor plans have been adjusted to accommodate larger showers and walk-in closets.

Working with Italy’s Ministry of Culture, the architects were also able to partially remove a kitchen wall, introducing a cocktail counter that connects the cooking and living areas. The opening allows natural light to reach further into the kitchen while creating a casual setting for gathering.

The material palette draws directly from Torre Velasca’s architecture. Working with Italian textile house Dedar, Matteo Thun & Partners developed custom velvet wall coverings in a dusty pink inspired by the building’s exterior plaster.

The color brings some of the tower’s character indoors, where it is paired with mustard-yellow sofas custom-designed for Molteni and coffee tables with distinctive stone finishes. Warm wood and deep green accents complete the interiors, giving the rooms a character that feels connected to Milan’s long history of furniture design.

An ecclectic collection of furnishings draw on several decades of Italian design, with pieces by Gio Ponti alongside work by Afra and Tobia Scarpa. Cassina’s Utrecht armchair appears in blue felt with contrasting green stitching, while lighting by Oluce has been produced in colors selected specifically for the apartments. Matteo Thun & Partners has also designed custom wardrobes and bedside furniture, manufactured by Italian producers.

Beyond the apartments, Matteo Thun & Partners has designed the reception and lobby spaces, as well as corridors toward the rear of the ground floor. The residences form part of a wider redevelopment that preserves Torre Velasca’s mixed-use character, with offices continuing to occupy the lower floors and hospitality spaces introduced throughout the building. The upper residences, operated as part of METT Milan Torre Velasca, extend this layout with accommodation for both shorter visits and longer stays.

From the street, Torre Velasca’s immense concrete brackets appear to support an entire block of apartments above the city. Inside, the rooms are surprisingly modest in scale. Their low ceilings and deep window openings are reminders of the building’s original design, even among the new furnishings. It is this contrast between the monumental exterior and the domestic spaces within that gives the project its particular character, allowing one of Milan’s most recognizable architectural landmarks to be experienced from the inside.

the apartments offer sweeping views across Milan, including the nearby Duomoa richly patterned counter introduces an informal gathering space beside the kitchen

Developers have revealed the challenges of getting the art style and gameplay right.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first tease of the The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake divided opinion with its revelation of what looked to be a highly realistic art style for one of Nintendo's most loved adventures. However, many fears will have been assuaged by the Zelda Ocarina of Time previews.

While the game is much more than a fresh coat of paint for the 1998 classic, with new controls, richer environments, extra dialogue, voiced cutscenes and fixes for some of the creakier bits of the original, it's also clear that Nintendo has been faithful to the original in many ways. Some of the thinking behind that comes across in a new series of interviews with developers. They reveal the vision for retaining a stylised look to the game's art, and confess that certain changes were considered but ruled out because they interfered with the core structure of the game.

As we noted in our preview, the new Hyrule of the Ocarina of Time remake remains very faithful to the shapes and colours of the N64 original but rebuilds them with sumptuous lighting and far more detail, from the grain in the wood and foliage to the stitching on Link’s tunic.

Despite the Nintendo Switch 2's far superior graphics capabilities compared to the N64, art director Aya Shida emphasises that the goal wasn't merely to make the classic look as realistic as possible. In early in development, the team used phrases like “a puppet-show feel” and “the analog feel of practical effects films” as concepts to aim for.

"We wanted to rebuild Hyrule as a rich, dense world that felt as though it could truly exist, while retaining the feel of the original. At the same time, we wanted its colorful and quirky characters to feel like a natural part of that world. Figuring out how to strike the right balance became one of the main themes of the art development," she says in Nintendo's Ask the Developer series.

"Neither puppet shows nor practical effects films reproduce reality exactly as it is. Even so, both create a convincing sense that the characters truly exist within their respective fantasy worlds," Aya adds.

The team began by drawing sketches of Link, Zelda and the other characters and creating a 3D model of the Great Deku Tree. Although the N64 designs and the new ones look very different due to the exaggerated features in the former, Aya says the aim was to preserve familiarity, which included paying particular consideration to how characters look from a distance "so that players would feel they were still the same characters they remembered, even after 28 years".

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

A lot of attention also went into the textures of the characters’ clothing. While they're much more detailed, they couldn't be took perfect. For example, the young Link's clothes needed to look handmade to be believable.

"We started by asking what kind of fabric those children might actually weave and wear," Aya reveals. "We looked at materials in museums and even experimented with making our own fabric from thread to get a better sense of what it should be like. For this game, the hardware allowed us to depict that level of detail, but that also meant we needed to do our research until we had a clear idea of what we wanted to create. As a design team, we often talked about imagining the story behind every object in the game as we created it."

While the objective was always to be faithful to the original game's focus on the joy of exploration, The Legend of Zelda series producer Eiji Aonuma reveals that the Ocarina of Time remake could have ended up with warp points like in Breath of the Wild.

"In the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, you could get around a bit faster by spamming forward roll, so I think a lot of players spent their time doggedly rolling across Hyrule Field whenever they needed to be somewhere in a hurry. I thought we needed to address this in this new version," he said.

However, developers discovered that adding the warp points to Ocarina of Time eliminated an important part of the game: the moments of discovery.

"Through this development process, we were reminded once again just how important those moments are to the very structure of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. So even though I was the one who proposed adding warp points, they just weren't working for me in the end, so I got the team to take them all back out again," he says.

One gameplay change that did make it into the remake is the addition of a dedicated jump button for Link, whereas he hopped automatically off certain ledges in the original. This will take some getting used to, especially mid-fight, but should be a welcome change for fiddly moments.

Eiji also commented on the reason for remaking Ocarina of Time in the first place as the franchise approached its 40th anniversary. He says that a significant part of the motivation was to ensure that the team working on the Zelda series today truly understands the original game's significance to the series as a whole.

"By learning the game structure and development style behind the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, and by actually rebuilding it as a full remake, it may trigger new insights that they can carry forward into future development," he suggests.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time launches on Nintendo Switch 2 on 5 November, 2026.

You can read the full interviews with developers on the Nintendo website.

#9122. European Beauty Standards: Impact on Self-Image and Diversity

Though we see flickers of progress come and go, European beauty standards — which essentially worship white physical features as the best — are still prevailing across popular culture.

Keep reading to learn more about the damaging beauty ideal. Plus, hear from Siena Liggins, an independent artist and songwriter, about how it affects the music industry and what’s necessary for change.

European beauty standards focus on specific physical features, including light skin and eyes, thin bodies and noses, and poker-straight hair, to name a few.

“It’s honestly just a trickle effect of something that just exists in our culture on a very wide scale,” Liggins says about European beauty standards.

The Western ideal defines beauty through thinness and whiteness, something American culture was all about for, you know, ever.

But beauty standards often shift in America, moving from one extreme like the rail-thin “heroin chic” look in the 90s to today’s adoration of big butts and busts, with a focus on exercise.

Still, whiteness remains the most represented ideal, and we still obsess over thin bodies, regularly debating which celebrities may or may not be on weight loss medication.

The impression the European beauty standards leave us with is that those who most closely match the call for light skin and eyes, thin noses, etc., are the best or most attractive people — leaving some people of color to internalize the messaging, resulting in feelings of self-hate.

This Western beauty ideal is not only exclusionary — shutting out Black, Indigenous, Arab, and Asian, Pacific Islander people — but it’s also deeply harmful.

The standard is unmistakably splashed across the entertainment and beauty industries, from not finding your makeup shade to not seeing your features represented in media.

It also penetrates our daily work and play, creating societal issues and difficulty with self-esteem that impacts everything from securing and keeping a job to socializing and education, starting as young as nursery school.

For one workplace example, a 2020 study found that white women or Black women with straightened hair are more likely to land job interviews than Black women wearing natural hairstyles like afros, twists, curls, or braids.

Some of the first research on skin color and self-perception among Black children included “the doll test.” Researchers presented Black children, aged 3–7, with four dolls that all looked the same — except for their skin color — and asked them a series of questions about which dolls were nicest or prettiest and which they liked best.

Two-thirds of the Black children chose the white doll. The test was repeated in a similar way in 2005, with 16 of the 21 preschool-aged Black children selecting the white doll.

Needless to say, the beauty standard also negatively impacts the educational system, romantic relationships, and a slew of other dynamics and environments.

“The reality is that you need people to challenge them if you’re ever going to see anything change,” Liggins says about beauty standards.

She points to “AMERICAN REQUIEM,” one song off Beyoncé’s country album Cowboy Carter.

“She talks about how for things to stay the same, they have to change again,” Liggins explains. Though she believes Beyoncé refers to a hope for peace and healing in the United States, Liggins says this concept can lend to beauty standards.

When it comes to the idealistic view that we put on celebrities and pop culture, Liggins says you have to reimagine what it looks like over and over again. “And what that requires is letting in new people, and it can’t just be from a vanity’s perspective,” Liggins says.

Coupled with who is represented in music videos, Liggins says change is also needed at a gatekeeper level. “It has to be the people who are coming up with the ideas and bringing them into fruition who also have to have diversity, not just a thought but of background, culture, and ethnicity,” she says.

Otherwise, Liggins says, we’ll only continue to see spikes in diversity, making inclusion more of a fad than a serious change.
